An annuity of coupons, plus the face value at the end. You priced both last week.

A 5-year bond, 4% coupon, face €100, yield 6%:
P = 4 \times 4.212364 + 74.73 = 16.85 + 74.73 = €91.58

title: What a rate rise costs you
section: Rates rise. Why is your old bond worth less?
text:
Rates rise. Why is your old bond worth less?

Same €100 at the end, €2 less every year. A buyer takes yours only at a discount: the price falls until your bond also earns 6% — that is the €91.58.

The rule that follows from the formula



coupon > yield
premium — price above face


coupon = yield

The bond pays 4% on its face; the market wants 6%. The only way to deliver 6% is to sell it for less than 100.
Price and yield move in opposite directions. Always, for every bond, with no exceptions.

title: What a rate rise costs you
section: Two durations, and the difference matters
text:
Two durations, and the difference matters


Macaulay — the average time to being repaid, weighted by present value: D = \sum_{t} t \cdot \frac{PV(CF_t)}{P} Measured in years.

Modified — the same thing turned into a sensitivity: D_{\text{mod}} = \frac{D}{1+y} = -\frac{1}{P}\frac{dP}{dy} Measured in % per 1% of yield.


\frac{\Delta P}{P} \;\approx\; -D_{\text{mod}} \times \Delta y
A 10-year 5% bond at par has D_mod = 7.72: a one-point rise in yields costs about 7.7% of its value.

Duration is how many percent you lose for each percent rates rise. It is one number, and it is the first one a Board asks for.

section: Can we stop worrying?
text:
Can we stop worrying?







Arno Bikes, a payment


The new building costs €1M, due in exactly 4 years. The firm sets the money aside today, in zero-coupon bonds yielding 5%. Then rates move.











Bet before we compute


Short bonds, long bonds, or a mix? Which choice leaves the €1M there in year 4, whichever way rates go?




Beyond the syllabus: the step after duration, from measuring the risk to removing it.

title: What a rate rise costs you
section: Rates rise. Two things happen at once.
text:
Rates rise. Two things happen at once.


Prices fall — bad
Whatever we still hold at year 4 is worth less. The longer the bond, the bigger the fall: that is duration.

Coupons reinvest at more — good
Whatever comes back before year 4 earns the higher rate until the payment. The sooner it comes back, the more it gains.


Short bonds: reinvestment wins. Long bonds: the price fall wins.
If the duration of what we hold equals the date of what we owe, the two effects offset — to first order.

title: What a rate rise costs you
section: Take home
text:
Take home

A bond is an annuity plus a lump sum. Price and yield move in opposite directions.
Duration is the slope: how many percent you lose per percent of yield.
Longer maturity raises it; a bigger coupon lowers it.
Convexity is the curvature the slope misses, and it is always in the holder’s favour.
Match the duration of what you hold to the date of what you owe, and a rate move cannot hurt the payment.
A study is seven steps, in the brief’s words; every number gets its sentence for the Board.

Step by step on a function you know
\pi(q) = -4q^{2} + 1200q - 60{,}000

Limits π(0) = −60,000; π(q) → −∞ as q → ∞. No asymptote: a polynomial has none.
Range (−∞, 30,000] — it reaches its maximum and never exceeds it.
Sign zeros at 63.4 and 236.6; positive between them.

title: Studying a function, and optimising it
section: Limits at the edge: where the curve runs off the page
text:
Limits at the edge: where the curve runs off the page
Step 2 asks for limits, and limits are how you find asymptotes — the lines the curve approaches and never meets. The resit asks for them by name.


Vertical. Look at the edge of the domain. f(q) = 7 ln(q + 3) is defined for q > −3, and
\lim_{q \to -3^{+}} 7\ln(q+3) = -\infty
so the line q = −3 is a vertical asymptote.

Horizontal. Look at infinity. AC(q) = 0.4q + 3 + 25/q has none: it grows without bound. But (60,000 + 400q)/q → 400, so y = 400 is one.

A sketch with no asymptote drawn, where one exists, is marked as an incomplete sketch.

title: Studying a function, and optimising it
section: Step 6 in the words of a report
text:
Step 6 in the words of a report
For the log-revenue firm of block B, R(q) = 30\ln(q+1), C(q) = 0.4q^{2} + 3q + 25:

C''(q) = 0.8 > 0: cost is convex throughout — each extra unit costs more than the last.
R''(q) = -30/(q+1)^{2} < 0: revenue is concave throughout — each extra unit brings in less than the last. Diminishing returns, by name.
So \pi'' = R'' - C'' < 0 everywhere: profit is concave, with a single maximum and no inflection. The optimum you find is the only one.








Board sentence


Convexity is the second thing a Board wants to know after the optimum: is the ground falling away on both sides fast or slowly. f'' is that number.

title: Studying a function, and optimising it
section: It is at the minimum, and that is not a coincidence
text:
It is at the minimum, and that is not a coincidence
C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25, so AC(q) = 0.4q + 3 + 25/q.
AC'(q) = 0.4 - \frac{25}{q^{2}} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; q^{2} = 62.5 \;\Rightarrow\; q \approx 7.91

There AC = 9.32 and C'(7.91) = 9.32. Equal.
While the next unit costs less than the average, it pulls the average down. When it costs more, it pushes it up. The average stops falling exactly when the two meet.

text:
The rule that runs every firm
\pi'(q) = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R'(q) = C'(q)
Produce up to the point where the revenue from one more unit equals what that unit costs.

For R(q) = 30 ln(q+1) and C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25:
\frac{30}{q+1} = 0.8q + 3 \;\Rightarrow\; 4q^{2} + 19q - 135 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; q \approx 3.90

title: Revision of mathematics, told as business decisions
section: An equation answers “where”. An inequality answers “from where on”.
text:
An equation answers “where”. An inequality answers “from where on”.
1{,}000q = 60{,}000 + 400q \;\Rightarrow\; q = 100 \qquad\qquad 1{,}000q \geq 60{,}000 + 400q \;\Rightarrow\; q \geq 100
The first is the break-even point. The second is the condition for not losing money — and it is the second one a Board asks for.
One rule, and it is the only one that costs marks: multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses it.

The question is not “how big is the cell” but “how far is it from 500”. That distance is the absolute value |c - 500|: never negative, whichever side you miss on.

text:
What |·| does to a graph





Everything below the axis is flipped up, like a mirror. Everything above stays where it is. So an absolute value is never negative, and its graph has a corner where the original crossed zero.

> — above the level: two tails, joined by “or”, never “and”.

Level below zero — a V never goes under the axis: no solution. With > it would be every x.

every 6 months   n =     2   €1,123.6000
every quarter    n =     4   €1,125.5088
every month      n =    12   €1,126.8250
every week       n =    52   €1,127.3410
every day        n =   365   €1,127.4746
every hour       n =  8760   €1,127.4959
continuously     n → ∞     €1,127.4969   ← the ceiling, and that is e



🔍 CHECK
The gap from yearly to daily is €7.47. The gap from daily to infinitely often is three cents. Say out loud what that means for a bank’s marketing.

B. The effective annual rate — the only honest comparison

def ear(nominal, m):
    return exp(nominal) - 1 if m is None else (1 + nominal/m)**m - 1

print("12% nominal:")
for lab, m in [("semi-annually", 2), ("quarterly", 4), ("monthly", 12), ("continuously", None)]:
    print(f"  compounded {lab:<14} EAR = {ear(0.12, m):.4%}")

print()
print("Bank A: 7.8% monthly  → EAR", f"{ear(0.078, 12):.4%}")
print("Bank B: 8.0% annually → EAR", f"{ear(0.08, 1):.4%}")
print("The lower headline rate is the dearer loan.")

  compounded quarterly      EAR = 12.5509%

The lower headline rate is the dearer loan.

title: MBA03 · Week 4 — Money has a date on it
section: Drills, solved in code
text:
Drills, solved in code
This section is an optional companion: the code is not examined, but it is a good way to check your work. Every drill from drills.md is solved here in plain Python, with the same numbers. Do the drill on paper first, then run the cell and compare.
D1 (a). €8,000 is invested for 3 years at 6% a year. Simple interest: the final amount.
\[A = P(1 + r\,t)\]

P = 8000     # principal, €
r = 0.06     # yearly rate
t = 3        # years

A_simple = P * (1 + r * t)    # interest only on the original €8,000
print(f"With simple interest the final amount is €{A_simple:,.2f}.")
assert abs(A_simple - 9440.00) < 0.01

With simple interest the final amount is €9,440.00.


D1 (b). Same money, compounded annually: the final amount.
\[A = P(1 + r)^t\]

P, r, t = 8000, 0.06, 3

A_compound = P * (1 + r) ** t    # interest also earns interest
print(f"Compounded annually the final amount is €{A_compound:,.2f}.")
assert abs(A_compound - 9528.13) < 0.01

Compounded annually the final amount is €9,528.13.


D1 (c). The difference, and one sentence on where it comes from.

P, r, t = 8000, 0.06, 3
A_simple = P * (1 + r * t)
A_compound = P * (1 + r) ** t

difference = A_compound - A_simple
print(f"Compounding earns €{difference:,.2f} more: interest is paid on the interest already earned.")
assert abs(difference - 88.13) < 0.01

Compounding earns €88.13 more: interest is paid on the interest already earned.


D2 (a). €5,000 for 4 years at 8% nominal, compounded quarterly. The final amount.
\[A = P\left(1 + \frac{i}{m}\right)^{m t}\]

P = 5000     # principal, €
i = 0.08     # nominal yearly rate
m = 4        # compounding periods per year (quarterly)
t = 4        # years

A = P * (1 + i / m) ** (m * t)    # 2% a quarter, 16 quarters
print(f"The final amount is €{A:,.2f}.")
assert abs(A - 6863.93) < 0.01

The final amount is €6,863.93.


D2 (b). The interest earned.

P, i, m, t = 5000, 0.08, 4, 4
A = P * (1 + i / m) ** (m * t)

interest = A - P
print(f"The interest earned is €{interest:,.2f}.")
assert abs(interest - 1863.93) < 0.01

The interest earned is €1,863.93.


D3. A bank quotes 6% nominal. Which is worth more to a depositor? (i) compounded annually (ii) compounded monthly (iii) they are the same

i = 0.06
ear_annual = (1 + i / 1) ** 1 - 1
ear_monthly = (1 + i / 12) ** 12 - 1

print(f"Annually: EAR = {ear_annual:.2%}.  Monthly: EAR = {ear_monthly:.2%}.")
print("Answer (ii): monthly compounding pays interest on interest sooner, so it is worth more.")
assert ear_monthly > ear_annual
assert abs(ear_monthly - 0.0617) < 0.00005

Annually: EAR = 6.00%.  Monthly: EAR = 6.17%.
Answer (ii): monthly compounding pays interest on interest sooner, so it is worth more.


D4. Compute the EAR for a 12% nominal rate compounded (a) semi-annually, (b) quarterly, (c) monthly.
\[\text{EAR} = \left(1 + \frac{i}{m}\right)^m - 1\]

i = 0.12
ear_a = (1 + i / 2) ** 2 - 1      # (a) semi-annually
ear_b = (1 + i / 4) ** 4 - 1      # (b) quarterly
ear_c = (1 + i / 12) ** 12 - 1    # (c) monthly

print(f"(a) semi-annually: EAR = {ear_a:.2%}")
print(f"(b) quarterly:     EAR = {ear_b:.2%}")
print(f"(c) monthly:       EAR = {ear_c:.2%}")
assert abs(ear_a - 0.1236) < 0.00005 and abs(ear_b - 0.1255) < 0.00005
assert abs(ear_c - 0.1268) < 0.00005

(a) semi-annually: EAR = 12.36%
(b) quarterly:     EAR = 12.55%
(c) monthly:       EAR = 12.68%


D4 (d). The same 12% compounded continuously.
\[\text{EAR} = e^{i} - 1\]

i = 0.12
ear_d = exp(i) - 1    # the ceiling that (a), (b), (c) approach

print(f"(d) continuously:  EAR = {ear_d:.2%} — the gaps shrink towards this ceiling.")
assert abs(ear_d - 0.1275) < 0.00005

(d) continuously:  EAR = 12.75% — the gaps shrink towards this ceiling.


D5. Bank A offers 7.8% compounded monthly. Bank B offers 8% compounded annually. Which do you borrow from, and why?

ear_A = (1 + 0.078 / 12) ** 12 - 1    # put Bank A on an annual basis
ear_B = (1 + 0.08 / 1) ** 1 - 1       # Bank B is already annual

print(f"Bank A: EAR = {ear_A:.3%}.  Bank B: EAR = {ear_B:.3%}.")
print("Borrow from B: A's lower quoted rate hides more frequent compounding.")
assert abs(ear_A - 0.08085) < 0.000005
assert ear_B < ear_A

Bank A: EAR = 8.085%.  Bank B: EAR = 8.000%.
Borrow from B: A's lower quoted rate hides more frequent compounding.


D6 (stretch). 5% nominal compounded continuously. What annual compounding rate leaves a depositor equally well off?

i = 0.05
equivalent_annual = exp(i) - 1    # one year of continuous growth, as a yearly rate

print(f"An annual rate of {equivalent_annual:.2%} is equivalent.")
assert abs(equivalent_annual - 0.0513) < 0.00005

An annual rate of 5.13% is equivalent.


D7. What is €10,000 receivable in 5 years worth today at 7%?
\[PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + r)^n}\]

FV = 10000   # € received in the future
r = 0.07
n = 5        # years away

PV = FV / (1 + r) ** n
print(f"€10,000 in 5 years is worth €{PV:,.2f} today.")
assert abs(PV - 7129.86) < 0.01

€10,000 in 5 years is worth €7,129.86 today.


D8. Pay for a €50,000 machine with (i) €50,000 today or (ii) €18,000 at the end of each of the next three years. Cost of capital 9%. Which do you choose?
\[PV_{\text{annuity}} = C \cdot \frac{1 - (1 + r)^{-n}}{r}\]

C, r, n = 18000, 0.09, 3
price_today = 50000

factor = (1 - (1 + r) ** -n) / r     # annuity factor
PV_instalments = C * factor
print(f"Annuity factor {factor:.6f}; PV of the instalments = €{PV_instalments:,.2f}.")
print(f"Pay in instalments: about €{price_today - PV_instalments:,.0f} less in today's money.")
assert abs(PV_instalments - 45563.31) < 0.02

Annuity factor 2.531295; PV of the instalments = €45,563.30.
Pay in instalments: about €4,437 less in today's money.


D9 (a). An annuity pays €12,000 at the end of each year for 10 years. At 6%, what is it worth today?

C, r, n = 12000, 0.06, 10

PV_annuity = C * (1 - (1 + r) ** -n) / r
print(f"The 10-year annuity is worth €{PV_annuity:,.2f} today.")
assert abs(PV_annuity - 88321.04) < 0.01

The 10-year annuity is worth €88,321.04 today.


D9 (b). A perpetuity pays €12,000 at the end of every year for ever. At 6%, what is it worth today?
\[PV = \frac{C}{r}\]

C, r = 12000, 0.06

PV_perpetuity = C / r
print(f"The perpetuity is worth €{PV_perpetuity:,.2f} today.")
assert abs(PV_perpetuity - 200000.00) < 0.01

The perpetuity is worth €200,000.00 today.


D9 (c). Explain the gap between (a) and (b).

C, r, n = 12000, 0.06, 10
PV_annuity = C * (1 - (1 + r) ** -n) / r
PV_perpetuity = C / r

gap = PV_perpetuity - PV_annuity    # value today of every payment after year 10
print(f"All the payments after year 10 are worth only €{gap:,.0f} today:")
print("discounting shrinks distant money towards nothing.")
assert abs(gap - 111679) < 1

All the payments after year 10 are worth only €111,679 today:
discounting shrinks distant money towards nothing.


D10 (core). A perpetuity pays €5,000 next year and grows at 2% a year for ever. At 7%, what is it worth today?
\[PV = \frac{C_1}{r - g}\]

C1 = 5000    # first payment, next year
r = 0.07     # discount rate
g = 0.02     # growth rate of the payment

PV = C1 / (r - g)
print(f"The growing perpetuity is worth €{PV:,.2f} today (€{C1/r:,.2f} with no growth).")
assert abs(PV - 100000.00) < 0.01

The growing perpetuity is worth €100,000.00 today (€71,428.57 with no growth).


D11 (a). What is Arno Bikes worth? Free cash flow €350k next year, growing 4% a year for ever, cost of capital 9%.
\[V = \frac{CF_1}{r - g}\]

CF1 = 350    # € thousand, next year
r, g = 0.09, 0.04

V = CF1 / (r - g)
print(f"Arno Bikes is worth €{V:,.2f}k today.")
assert abs(V - 7000.00) < 0.01

Arno Bikes is worth €7,000.00k today.


D11 (b). By how much does the value change if growth is one point lower (3% instead of 4%)?

CF1, r = 350, 0.09
V4 = CF1 / (r - 0.04)
V3 = CF1 / (r - 0.03)

change = V3 - V4
print(f"At 3% the value is €{V3:,.2f}k: a change of €{change:,.2f}k, or {change/V4:.2%}.")
assert abs(V3 - 5833.33) < 0.01 and abs(change - (-1166.67)) < 0.01 and abs(change/V4 + 0.1667) < 0.00005

At 3% the value is €5,833.33k: a change of €-1,166.67k, or -16.67%.


D11 (c). One sentence for the Board.

CF1, r = 350, 0.09
V4, V3 = CF1 / (r - 0.04), CF1 / (r - 0.03)
print(f"On our forecast Arno Bikes is worth about €{V4/1000:.1f}M; if growth is one point lower it is worth "
      f"€{V3/1000:.1f}M, so the price should rest on the growth we can defend, not the one we hope for.")
assert round(V4/1000, 1) == 7.0 and round(V3/1000, 1) == 5.8

On our forecast Arno Bikes is worth about €7.0M; if growth is one point lower it is worth €5.8M, so the price should rest on the growth we can defend, not the one we hope for.


D12 (stretch). A listed rival is valued at €12M; next year’s free cash flow is €600k; cost of capital 9%. What growth for ever is the market pricing in?
\[P = \frac{CF_1}{r - g} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = r - \frac{CF_1}{P}\]

P = 12000    # € thousand, market value
CF1 = 600    # € thousand, next year
r = 0.09

g_implied = r - CF1 / P
print(f"The market is pricing in growth of {g_implied:.2%} a year for ever.")
assert abs(g_implied - 0.04) < 1e-9
assert abs(CF1 / (r - g_implied) - P) < 1e-6    # plug it back: the formula returns the price

The market is pricing in growth of 4.00% a year for ever.


D13 (a). Arno Bikes’ assembly line at a 9% cost of capital: write the NPV as a sum (€ thousand).
\[NPV = -2400 + \frac{700}{1.09} + \frac{800}{1.09^2} + \frac{900}{1.09^3} + \frac{1000}{1.09^4}\]

flows = [-2400, 700, 800, 900, 1000]    # € thousand, years 0..4
r = 0.09

terms = [f"{cf}/(1.09)^{t}" for t, cf in enumerate(flows)]
print("NPV = " + " + ".join(terms))

NPV = -2400/(1.09)^0 + 700/(1.09)^1 + 800/(1.09)^2 + 900/(1.09)^3 + 1000/(1.09)^4


D13 (b). Compute each discounted flow and the NPV.

flows = [-2400, 700, 800, 900, 1000]    # € thousand
r = 0.09

table = pd.DataFrame({"Year": range(len(flows)), "Flow (€k)": flows})
table["Factor"] = 1 / (1 + r) ** table["Year"]
table["Present value (€k)"] = table["Flow (€k)"] * table["Factor"]
print(table.round({"Factor": 6, "Present value (€k)": 2}).to_string(index=False))

NPV = table["Present value (€k)"].sum()
print(f"NPV = €{NPV:,.2f}k")
assert abs(NPV - 318.94) < 0.01

 Year  Flow (€k)   Factor  Present value (€k)
    0      -2400 1.000000            -2400.00
    1        700 0.917431              642.20
    2        800 0.841680              673.34
    3        900 0.772183              694.97
    4       1000 0.708425              708.43
NPV = €318.94k


D13 (c). Accept or reject, and say the sentence you would tell the Board.

flows = [-2400, 700, 800, 900, 1000]
r = 0.09
NPV = sum(cf / (1 + r) ** t for t, cf in enumerate(flows))

decision = "Accept" if NPV > 0 else "Reject"
print(f"{decision}. At our 9% cost of capital the line adds about €{round(NPV)*1000:,.0f}")
print("of value in today's money.")
assert decision == "Accept"

Accept. At our 9% cost of capital the line adds about €319,000
of value in today's money.


D13b (a). 60% equity, 40% debt. Shareholders expect 12%, the bank charges 6%, tax rate 25%. Compute the WACC.
\[\text{WACC} = w_e\,r_e + w_d\,r_d\,(1 - T)\]

w_e, w_d = 0.60, 0.40    # weights of equity and debt
r_e, r_d = 0.12, 0.06    # cost of equity, cost of debt
T = 0.25                 # corporate tax rate

WACC = w_e * r_e + w_d * r_d * (1 - T)
print(f"WACC = {w_e*r_e:.1%} + {w_d*r_d*(1-T):.1%} = {WACC:.1%} — the 9% we were handed.")
assert abs(WACC - 0.09) < 1e-9

WACC = 7.2% + 1.8% = 9.0% — the 9% we were handed.


D13b (b). Why does the tax rate appear at all, and only on the debt side?

r_d, T = 0.06, 0.25

after_tax_debt = r_d * (1 - T)    # interest is deductible from taxable profit
print(f"Interest is tax-deductible, so a 6% loan really costs {after_tax_debt:.1%} after tax.")
print("Dividends are not deductible, so the equity side gets no (1 - T).")
assert abs(after_tax_debt - 0.045) < 1e-9

Interest is tax-deductible, so a 6% loan really costs 4.5% after tax.
Dividends are not deductible, so the equity side gets no (1 - T).


D13b (c). If the mix became 40/60 (more debt), what happens to the WACC and to the NPV of the line?

r_e, r_d, T = 0.12, 0.06, 0.25
flows = [-2400, 700, 800, 900, 1000]
npv = lambda r: sum(cf / (1 + r) ** t for t, cf in enumerate(flows))

WACC_new = 0.40 * r_e + 0.60 * r_d * (1 - T)    # more weight on the cheaper source
print(f"WACC falls from 9.0% to {WACC_new:.1%}; NPV rises from €{npv(0.09):,.2f}k to €{npv(WACC_new):,.2f}k.")
print("Not free: more debt means more risk, and in time r_e and r_d rise with it.")
assert WACC_new < 0.09 and npv(WACC_new) > npv(0.09)

WACC falls from 9.0% to 7.5%; NPV rises from €318.94k to €416.69k.
Not free: more debt means more risk, and in time r_e and r_d rise with it.


D14 (stretch). Recompute the NPV at 16%. What does the change in sign tell you, and what is the rate at which it happens?

flows = [-2400, 700, 800, 900, 1000]    # € thousand
npv = lambda r: sum(cf / (1 + r) ** t for t, cf in enumerate(flows))
print(f"NPV at 16% = −€{-npv(0.16):,.2f}k: negative.")

lo, hi = 0.09, 0.16            # NPV > 0 at 9%, < 0 at 16%: the zero is in between
for _ in range(50):            # bisection: halve the interval, keep the sign change
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    lo, hi = (mid, hi) if npv(mid) > 0 else (lo, mid)
irr = (lo + hi) / 2
print(f"NPV = 0 at {irr:.1%}: the internal rate of return. Above it the project destroys value.")
assert abs(npv(0.16) - (-73.14)) < 0.01 and abs(irr - 0.146) < 0.0005

NPV at 16% = −€73.14k: negative.
NPV = 0 at 14.6%: the internal rate of return. Above it the project destroys value.

import numpy as np, plotly.graph_objects as go, sympy as sp

print("ready")

section: A. Domain — where a function means anything
text:
A. Domain — where a function means anything
The exam asks “state the domain” and wants an interval. Sympy agrees with you or it does not.

for expr in (sp.sqrt(q - 20), sp.log(q - 5), 120/(q - 40)):
    print(f"{str(expr):<18} domain: {sp.calculus.util.continuous_domain(expr, q, sp.S.Reals)}")

sqrt(q - 20)       domain: Interval(20, oo)
log(q - 5)         domain: Interval.open(5, oo)
120/(q - 40)       domain: Union(Interval.open(-oo, 40), Interval.open(40, oo))

section: B. Limits — near a point you cannot reach
text:
B. Limits — near a point you cannot reach
Average cost at zero output is undefined. Near zero, and far out, it is not.

AC = (60000 + 400*q)/q
print("as q -> 0+ :", sp.limit(AC, q, 0, "+"))
print("as q -> oo :", sp.limit(AC, q, sp.oo))
print()
print("(q^2-100)/(q-10) as q->10 :", sp.limit((q**2 - 100)/(q - 10), q, 10))
print("(q-1)^2/(q-q^2)  as q->1+ :", sp.limit((q - 1)**2/(q - q**2), q, 1, "+"))

as q -> 0+ : oo
as q -> oo : 400

(q^2-100)/(q-10) as q->10 : 20
(q-1)^2/(q-q^2)  as q->1+ : 0



🔍 CHECK
The second one is 0/0. Factor it by hand first, then compare. If your hand answer and sympy disagree, sympy is not the one that is wrong — but find out where you diverged before moving on.

title: MBA03 · Week 2 — The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: C. The derivative — what does one more bike do?
text:
C. The derivative — what does one more bike do?
Move the point along the curve and read the slope. The slope is the answer to the only question a manager asks about the next unit.

profit = lambda x: -4*x**2 + 1200*x - 60000
prime  = lambda x: -8*x + 1200
qs = np.linspace(0, 300, 400)

frames, points = [], np.arange(20, 281, 10)
for q0 in points:
    xs = np.linspace(q0 - 60, q0 + 60, 2)
    frames.append(go.Frame(name=str(q0), data=[
        go.Scatter(x=qs, y=profit(qs), line=dict(color="#363636", width=3)),
        go.Scatter(x=xs, y=profit(q0) + prime(q0)*(xs - q0), line=dict(color="#AF1F25", width=3)),
        go.Scatter(x=[q0], y=[profit(q0)], mode="markers+text", marker=dict(size=12, color="#AF1F25"),
                   text=[f"π'({q0}) = {prime(q0):+,.0f}"], textposition="top center"),
    ]))

fig = go.Figure(data=frames[0].data, frames=frames)
fig.update_layout(
    template="simple_white", height=480, showlegend=False,
    xaxis_title="bikes per month  q", yaxis_title="profit €",
    xaxis_range=[0, 300], yaxis_range=[-70000, 45000],
    sliders=[dict(active=0, currentvalue=dict(prefix="q = "),
                  steps=[dict(method="animate", label=f.name,
                              args=[[f.name], dict(mode="immediate", frame=dict(duration=0, redraw=True))])
                         for f in frames])])
fig.show()

Unable to display output for mime type(s): application/vnd.plotly.v1+json


Watch the sign, not the number. Positive: make more. Negative: make fewer. Zero: you are at the top.

pi = -4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000
print("π'(q) =", sp.diff(pi, q))
print("π'(80)  =", sp.diff(pi, q).subs(q, 80), " → one more bike adds about €560")
print("π'(200) =", sp.diff(pi, q).subs(q, 200), " → one more bike costs about €400")
print("π'(q) = 0 at q =", sp.solve(sp.diff(pi, q), q))
print("week 1's vertex -b/2a =", -1200/(2*-4))

π'(q) = 1200 - 8*q
π'(80)  = 560  → one more bike adds about €560
π'(200) = -400  → one more bike costs about €400
π'(q) = 0 at q = [150]
week 1's vertex -b/2a = 150.0



Change one number and watch everything move
The price falls €4 for each extra bike. What if it fell €3? Or €6?

for drop in (3, 4, 6):
    p = (1600 - drop*q)*q - (60000 + 400*q)
    qstar = sp.solve(sp.diff(p, q), q)[0]
    print(f"price drop €{drop}/bike → best quantity {float(qstar):6.1f}, profit €{float(p.subs(q, qstar)):>10,.0f}")

price drop €3/bike → best quantity  200.0, profit €    60,000
price drop €4/bike → best quantity  150.0, profit €    30,000
price drop €6/bike → best quantity  100.0, profit €         0

title: MBA03 · Week 2 — The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: D. Running it backwards
text:
D. Running it backwards
Given the derivative, recover the function. The constant is not decoration.

c = sp.Symbol("c")
F = sp.integrate(6*q**2 - 2*q, q)
k = sp.solve(sp.Eq((F + c).subs(q, 1), 4), c)[0]
print("f'(q) = 6q² − 2q, f(1) = 4  →  f(q) =", F + k)

MC = sp.Rational(8, 10)*q + 3
print("MC(q) = 0.8q + 3 with C(0) = 25  →  C(q) =", sp.integrate(MC, q) + 25)
print("...and the constant IS the fixed cost.")

f'(q) = 6q² − 2q, f(1) = 4  →  f(q) = 2*q**3 - q**2 + 3
MC(q) = 0.8q + 3 with C(0) = 25  →  C(q) = 2*q**2/5 + 3*q + 25
...and the constant IS the fixed cost.

title: MBA03 · Week 2 — The tool that finds the top of any hill
section: Drills, solved in code
text:
Drills, solved in code
This section is an optional companion: the code is not examined, but it is a good way to check your work. Every drill from drills.md is solved here with sympy, step by step, the way you would solve it by hand. Do the drill on paper first, then run the cell and compare.
D1 (a) State the domain of \(f(q) = \sqrt{q - 20}\).

from sympy import solve_univariate_inequality
# A square root needs a non-negative inside
domain = solve_univariate_inequality(q - 20 >= 0, q, relational=False)
print("Domain of sqrt(q - 20):", domain)
assert domain == sp.Interval(20, sp.oo)

Domain of sqrt(q - 20): Interval(20, oo)


D1 (b) State the domain of \(g(q) = \ln(q - 5)\).

# A logarithm needs a strictly positive inside (ln 0 does not exist)
domain = solve_univariate_inequality(q - 5 > 0, q, relational=False)
print("Domain of ln(q - 5):", domain)
assert domain == sp.Interval.open(5, sp.oo)

Domain of ln(q - 5): Interval.open(5, oo)


D1 (c) State the domain of \(h(q) = \dfrac{120}{q - 40}\).

# A fraction needs a denominator different from zero
domain = solve_univariate_inequality(sp.Ne(q - 40, 0), q, relational=False)
print("Domain of 120/(q - 40):", domain)
# For a quantity we also need q >= 0
print("For a quantity:", domain.intersect(sp.Interval(0, sp.oo)))
assert domain == sp.Union(sp.Interval.open(-sp.oo, 40), sp.Interval.open(40, sp.oo))

Domain of 120/(q - 40): Union(Interval.open(-oo, 40), Interval.open(40, oo))
For a quantity: Union(Interval.Ropen(0, 40), Interval.open(40, oo))


D2 (a) Arno Bikes faces demand \(p(q) = 1600 - 4q\). Write revenue \(R(q)\) and simplify.

price = 1600 - 4*q
R = sp.expand(price * q)          # revenue = price x quantity
print("R(q) =", R)
assert R == 1600*q - 4*q**2

R(q) = -4*q**2 + 1600*q


D2 (b) Write profit \(\pi(q)\) using \(C(q) = 60{,}000 + 400q\).

C = 60000 + 400*q
pi_q = sp.expand(R - C)           # profit = revenue - cost
print("π(q) =", pi_q)
assert pi_q == -4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000

π(q) = -4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000


D2 (c) Evaluate \(\pi(100)\) and \(\pi(200)\). Which quantity is better, and by how much?

p100 = int(pi_q.subs(q, 100))
p200 = int(pi_q.subs(q, 200))
print(f"π(100) = €{p100:,}   π(200) = €{p200:,}   difference = €{p200 - p100:,}")
print("They are equal: the parabola is symmetric about q = 150.")
assert p100 == 20000 and p200 == 20000

π(100) = €20,000   π(200) = €20,000   difference = €0
They are equal: the parabola is symmetric about q = 150.


D3 (a) A second firm has \(R(q) = 30\ln(q + 1)\) (€ thousand). State the domain of \(R\) for \(q \ge 0\).

# The log needs q + 1 > 0; then keep only quantities q >= 0
domain = solve_univariate_inequality(q + 1 > 0, q, relational=False)
domain_q = domain.intersect(sp.Interval(0, sp.oo))
print("Domain of 30 ln(q + 1):", domain, "  for a quantity:", domain_q)
assert domain_q == sp.Interval(0, sp.oo)

Domain of 30 ln(q + 1): Interval.open(-1, oo)   for a quantity: Interval(0, oo)


D3 (b) With \(C(q) = 0.4q^2 + 3q + 25\), compute \(\pi(5)\) and \(\pi(10)\) to two decimals.

R2 = 30*sp.log(q + 1)
C2 = sp.Rational(4, 10)*q**2 + 3*q + 25
profit2 = R2 - C2
pi5 = round(float(profit2.subs(q, 5)), 2)
pi10 = round(float(profit2.subs(q, 10)), 2)
print(f"π(5) = €{pi5}k   π(10) = €{pi10}k  → past its best scale at 10")
assert pi5 == 3.75
assert pi10 == -23.06   # 30 ln 11 = 71.94, so 71.94 - 95 = -23.06

π(5) = €3.75k   π(10) = €-23.06k  → past its best scale at 10


D4 (a) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to 10} \frac{q^2 - 100}{q - 10}\), showing the factoring step.

expr = (q**2 - 100)/(q - 10)
print("numerator factored:", sp.factor(q**2 - 100))
print("after cancelling:  ", sp.cancel(expr))
answer = sp.limit(expr, q, 10)
print("The limit as q → 10 is", answer)
assert answer == 20

numerator factored: (q - 10)*(q + 10)
after cancelling:   q + 10
The limit as q → 10 is 20


D4 (b) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to 3} \frac{q^2 - 5q + 6}{q - 3}\), showing the factoring step.

expr = (q**2 - 5*q + 6)/(q - 3)
print("numerator factored:", sp.factor(q**2 - 5*q + 6))
print("after cancelling:  ", sp.cancel(expr))
answer = sp.limit(expr, q, 3)
print("The limit as q → 3 is", answer)
assert answer == 1

numerator factored: (q - 3)*(q - 2)
after cancelling:   q - 2
The limit as q → 3 is 1


D5 Evaluate the one-sided limit \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to 1^+} \frac{(q - 1)^2}{q - q^2}\).

expr = (q - 1)**2/(q - q**2)
print("denominator factored:", sp.factor(q - q**2))   # -q(q - 1)
print("after cancelling:    ", sp.cancel(expr))       # -(q - 1)/q
answer = sp.limit(expr, q, 1, dir="+")                # from above only
print("The limit as q → 1 from above is", answer)
assert answer == 0

denominator factored: -q*(q - 1)
after cancelling:     (1 - q)/q
The limit as q → 1 from above is 0


D6 (a) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to\infty} \frac{1200q - 4q^2}{q^2}\) and say what it means for the firm.

expr = (1200*q - 4*q**2)/q**2
print("divided through by q²:", sp.expand(expr))    # 1200/q - 4
answer = sp.limit(expr, q, sp.oo)
print("The limit is", answer, "→ far out, the -4q² term dominates: deep loss.")
assert answer == -4

divided through by q²: -4 + 1200/q
The limit is -4 → far out, the -4q² term dominates: deep loss.


D6 (b) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to\infty} \frac{60{,}000 + 400q}{q}\) — average cost per bike as the run gets long.

AC = (60000 + 400*q)/q
print("split the fraction:", sp.expand(AC))          # 60000/q + 400
answer = sp.limit(AC, q, sp.oo)
print(f"Average cost settles at €{answer} per bike: fixed cost spreads to nothing.")
assert answer == 400

split the fraction: 400 + 60000/q
Average cost settles at €400 per bike: fixed cost spreads to nothing.


D7 Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{q\to -\infty} \frac{3q^3 - 2q + 1}{5q^3 + q^2}\).

expr = (3*q**3 - 2*q + 1)/(5*q**3 + q**2)
# Divide top and bottom by q³: every other term goes to 0
answer = sp.limit(expr, q, -sp.oo)
print("The limit as q → -∞ is", answer, "(ratio of the leading coefficients)")
assert answer == sp.Rational(3, 5)

The limit as q → -∞ is 3/5 (ratio of the leading coefficients)


D8 Differentiate, term by term: (a) \(\pi(q) = -4q^2 + 1200q - 60{,}000\) (b) \(C(q) = 0.4q^2 + 3q + 25\) (c) \(R(q) = 30\ln(q + 1)\) (d) \(f(q) = 5q^3 - 2q^2 + 7q - 1\)

d_a = sp.diff(-4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000, q)
d_b = sp.diff(sp.Rational(4, 10)*q**2 + 3*q + 25, q)
d_c = sp.diff(30*sp.log(q + 1), q)
d_d = sp.diff(5*q**3 - 2*q**2 + 7*q - 1, q)
print("(a) π'(q) =", d_a, "  (b) C'(q) =", d_b)
print("(c) R'(q) =", d_c, "  (d) f'(q) =", d_d)
assert d_a == -8*q + 1200 and d_b == sp.Rational(8, 10)*q + 3
assert d_c == 30/(q + 1) and d_d == 15*q**2 - 4*q + 7

(a) π'(q) = 1200 - 8*q   (b) C'(q) = 4*q/5 + 3
(c) R'(q) = 30/(q + 1)   (d) f'(q) = 15*q**2 - 4*q + 7


D8b Differentiate, naming the inside each time: (a) \(\ln(q + 1)\) (b) \(\ln(5q)\) (c) \((3q - 4)^5\) (d) \(e^{0.08t}\) (e) \(20\ln(2q + 7)\)

t = sp.Symbol("t", real=True)
d_a = sp.diff(sp.log(q + 1), q)                  # inside q + 1, times 1
d_b = sp.simplify(sp.diff(sp.log(5*q), q))       # inside 5q, times 5
d_c = sp.diff((3*q - 4)**5, q)                   # inside 3q - 4, times 3
d_d = sp.diff(sp.exp(0.08*t), t)                 # inside 0.08t, times 0.08
d_e = sp.diff(20*sp.log(2*q + 7), q)             # inside 2q + 7, times 2
print("(a)", d_a, " (b)", d_b, " (c)", d_c, " (d)", d_d, " (e)", d_e)
assert (d_a, d_b, d_c) == (1/(q + 1), 1/q, 15*(3*q - 4)**4)
assert d_d == 0.08*sp.exp(0.08*t) and d_e == 40/(2*q + 7)

(a) 1/(q + 1)  (b) 1/q  (c) 15*(3*q - 4)**4  (d) 0.08*exp(0.08*t)  (e) 40/(2*q + 7)


D9 (a) For \(\pi(q) = -4q^2 + 1200q - 60{,}000\), compute \(\pi'(80)\) and say what it means for a manager.

marginal = sp.diff(-4*q**2 + 1200*q - 60000, q)   # -8q + 1200
m80 = marginal.subs(q, 80)
print(f"π'(80) = {m80}: at 80 bikes a month, one more bike adds about €{m80} to profit. Make more.")
assert m80 == 560

π'(80) = 560: at 80 bikes a month, one more bike adds about €560 to profit. Make more.


D9 (b) Compute \(\pi'(200)\) and say what it means.

m200 = marginal.subs(q, 200)
print(f"π'(200) = {m200}: at 200 bikes, one more bike costs about €{-m200} of profit. Make fewer.")
assert m200 == -400

π'(200) = -400: at 200 bikes, one more bike costs about €400 of profit. Make fewer.


D9 (c) Solve \(\pi'(q) = 0\) and compare with the week-1 vertex \(-b/2a\).

q_best = sp.solve(sp.Eq(marginal, 0), q)[0]
vertex = sp.Rational(-1200, 2*(-4))                # -b / 2a from week 1
print(f"π'(q) = 0 at q = {q_best}; the week-1 vertex is q = {vertex}. Same point.")
assert q_best == 150 and vertex == 150

π'(q) = 0 at q = 150; the week-1 vertex is q = 150. Same point.


D10 Using the definition \(f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\), show that the derivative of \(f(q) = 3q^2\) at \(q = a\) is \(6a\).

a, h = sp.symbols("a h", real=True)
f = lambda x: 3*x**2
quotient = (f(a + h) - f(a))/h
print("difference quotient, simplified:", sp.cancel(quotient))   # 6a + 3h
answer = sp.limit(quotient, h, 0)
print("Letting h → 0, f'(a) =", answer)
assert answer == 6*a

difference quotient, simplified: 6*a + 3*h
Letting h → 0, f'(a) = 6*a


D11 Find \(f(q)\) given \(f'(q) = 6q^2 - 2q\) and \(f(1) = 4\).

c = sp.Symbol("c")
f = sp.integrate(6*q**2 - 2*q, q) + c          # antiderivative + constant
print("general solution: f(q) =", f)
c_value = sp.solve(sp.Eq(f.subs(q, 1), 4), c)[0]   # use f(1) = 4
f = f.subs(c, c_value)
print(f"f(1) = 4 gives c = {c_value}, so f(q) = {f}")
assert sp.expand(f - (2*q**3 - q**2 + 3)) == 0

general solution: f(q) = c + 2*q**3 - q**2
f(1) = 4 gives c = 3, so f(q) = 2*q**3 - q**2 + 3


D12 Find the total cost function given marginal cost \(MC(q) = 0.8q + 3\) and fixed cost \(C(0) = 25\).

c = sp.Symbol("c")
C = sp.integrate(sp.Rational(8, 10)*q + 3, q) + c   # antiderivative + constant
c_value = sp.solve(sp.Eq(C.subs(q, 0), 25), c)[0]   # use C(0) = 25
C = C.subs(c, c_value)
print(f"C(0) = 25 gives c = {c_value}, so C(q) = {C}. The constant IS the fixed cost.")
assert sp.expand(C - (sp.Rational(4, 10)*q**2 + 3*q + 25)) == 0

C(0) = 25 gives c = 25, so C(q) = 2*q**2/5 + 3*q + 25. The constant IS the fixed cost.


D13 Integrate: (a) \(\int (6q^2 - 4q + 1)\,dq\); (b) \(\int \frac{3q^3 + 4q^2 - 2}{q}\,dq\).

F_a = sp.integrate(6*q**2 - 4*q + 1, q)
print("(a)", F_a, "+ c")
split = sp.expand((3*q**3 + 4*q**2 - 2)/q)      # divide every term by q first
F_b = sp.integrate(split, q)
print("(b) split:", split, "  ->  integral:", F_b, "+ c")
assert sp.expand(F_a - (2*q**3 - 2*q**2 + q)) == 0
assert sp.simplify(sp.diff(F_b, q) - (3*q**3 + 4*q**2 - 2)/q) == 0   # differentiate back

(a) 2*q**3 - 2*q**2 + q + c
(b) split: 3*q**2 + 4*q - 2/q   ->  integral: q**3 + 2*q**2 - 2*log(q) + c


D3b \(C(q) = 0.6q^2 + 4q + 15\), \(R(q) = 25\ln(0.5q + 1)\): domains, axes, and the vertex of \(C\).

C3 = sp.Rational(3, 5)*q**2 + 4*q + 15
R3 = 25*sp.log(q/2 + 1)
dom_R = solve_univariate_inequality(q/2 + 1 > 0, q, relational=False)
print("algebraic domain of R:", dom_R, "  economic domain of both: [0, oo)")
disc = 4**2 - 4*sp.Rational(3, 5)*15
vertex = sp.solve(sp.diff(C3, q), q)[0]
print("C(0) =", C3.subs(q, 0), "(fixed cost);  discriminant of C =", disc, "-> no zero")
print("R(0) =", R3.subs(q, 0), "-> through the origin;  vertex of C at q =", vertex, "outside [0, oo)")
assert dom_R == sp.Interval.open(-2, sp.oo) and disc == -20 and C3.subs(q, 0) == 15
assert R3.subs(q, 0) == 0 and vertex == sp.Rational(-10, 3)

algebraic domain of R: Interval.open(-2, oo)   economic domain of both: [0, oo)
C(0) = 15 (fixed cost);  discriminant of C = -20 -> no zero
R(0) = 0 -> through the origin;  vertex of C at q = -10/3 outside [0, oo)


D7b Slant asymptotes: \(m = \lim f(q)/q\), then \(b = \lim (f(q) - mq)\).

x = sp.Symbol('x', real=True)
cases = {"C": C3, "R": R3, "AC": C3/q, "f": (2*x**2 + 3*x - 1)/(x + 1)}
found = {}
for name, f in cases.items():
    v = x if name == "f" else q
    m = sp.limit(f/v, v, sp.oo)
    b = sp.limit(f - m*v, v, sp.oo) if m.is_finite and m != 0 else None
    found[name] = (m, b)
    print(f"{name}: m = {m}, b = {b}", "-> y = %s·q + %s" % (m, b) if b is not None and b.is_finite else "-> no slant asymptote")
assert found["C"][0] == sp.oo and found["R"][0] == 0
assert found["AC"] == (sp.Rational(3, 5), 4) and found["f"] == (2, 1)

C: m = oo, b = None -> no slant asymptote
R: m = 0, b = None -> no slant asymptote
AC: m = 3/5, b = 4 -> y = 3/5·q + 4
f: m = 2, b = 1 -> y = 2·q + 1

text:
Homework

title: Reading week — The full mock: weeks 1–5 in one sitting
text:
For the reading week, at home. About three hours in all; do it in two sittings if you prefer. Exam conditions: no notes, non-programmable calculator only, all work shown.
This is not a real paper. It is this course, end to end, the way we have done it in class: the final’s calculus question twice, a full study of a function, and then Arno Bikes again — a new product line, a duty on its parts, the money it ties up, and a market abroad that closes its doors. Every function and number is new. Solutions are folded at the bottom of each part; mark yourself honestly, one part at a time.









part

A
the final’s calculus question, twice: five items each
2 × 30’
weeks 2–3

a full study of a function, with asymptotes
30’

Arno Bikes makes its own batteries — and the cells get a duty
45’
weeks 1–3; week-3 addendum, block C


D
Arno Bikes’ money: interest, discounting, the battery project, a bond

Arno Bikes’ export market puts up a tariff — optional
15’
week-3 addendum, block D



Marks are for method. A correct answer with no working scores badly; a wrong answer with sound working scores well.



Each set is five items, 20% each, thirty minutes.


A1. Evaluate, splitting the fraction first: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{6x^{2} - 4x + 3}{x}\,dx\)
A2. Find f(x) given \(f'(x) = 9x^{2} - 8x + 2\) and \(f(-1) = 4\).
A3. Evaluate, factoring and commenting on the sign of each factor: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} \frac{x^{2} - 5x + 6}{x^{2} - 2x}\)
A4. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{5x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} + x - 1}\)
A5. Evaluate, leaving the answer in terms of ln: \(\displaystyle\int_{2}^{4} \left(\frac{3}{x} + \frac{2x}{x^{2} - 3}\right) dx\)



A6. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \frac{2x^{3} + 5x - 4}{x^{2}}\,dx\)
A7. Find f(x) given \(f'(x) = 4x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 1\) and \(f(2) = 7\).
A8. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} \frac{x^{2} - 9}{x^{2} - 6x + 9}\)
A9. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{3x^{3} + 2x}{x^{2} - 4}\)
A10. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \left(\frac{2}{x + 1} + \frac{4x}{x^{2} + 1}\right) dx\)


Solutions to part A

A1. Split: \(6x - 4 + \dfrac{3}{x}\). Integrate term by term: \(3x^{2} - 4x + 3\ln|x| + c\).
A2. \(f(x) = 3x^{3} - 4x^{2} + 2x + c\). Then \(f(-1) = -3 - 4 - 2 + c = -9 + c = 4\), so \(c = 13\): \(f(x) = 3x^{3} - 4x^{2} + 2x + 13\). Every sign of \((-1)^{n}\) written out: odd powers stay negative.
A3. Substituting gives \(0/0\): factor. \(\dfrac{(x-2)(x-3)}{x(x-2)} = \dfrac{x-3}{x}\) for \(x \neq 2\). As \(x \to 2^{+}\), \(x - 3 \to -1\) and \(x \to 2\): the limit is \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\). The one-sided approach does not change the answer here, because the factor that vanished has cancelled.
A4. Divide by \(x^{2}\): \(\dfrac{5 - 3/x}{2 + 1/x - 1/x^{2}} \to\) \(\tfrac{5}{2}\). Same degree top and bottom: the ratio of the leading coefficients.
A5. \(\int \frac{3}{x}dx = 3\ln|x|\); the second term has the derivative of its denominator on top: \(\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-3}dx = \ln|x^{2} - 3|\). \(\big[3\ln x + \ln(x^{2} - 3)\big]_{2}^{4} = (3\ln 4 + \ln 13) - (3\ln 2 + \ln 1) = 3\ln 2 + \ln 13 =\) \(\ln 104 \approx 4.644\).
A6. Split: \(2x + \dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{4}{x^{2}} = 2x + 5x^{-1} - 4x^{-2}\). Integrate: \(x^{2} + 5\ln|x| + \dfrac{4}{x} + c\) (since \(\int -4x^{-2}dx = 4x^{-1}\)).
A7. \(f(x) = x^{4} - 2x^{3} + x + c\); \(f(2) = 16 - 16 + 2 + c = 7\), so \(c = 5\): \(f(x) = x^{4} - 2x^{3} + x + 5\).
A8. \(\dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x-3)^{2}} = \dfrac{x+3}{x-3}\). As \(x \to 3^{-}\): the top \(\to 6 > 0\), the bottom \(\to 0\) through negative values. Positive over a vanishing negative: \(-\infty\). A vertical asymptote at \(x = 3\); from the right the limit is \(+\infty\).
A9. The top has the higher degree. Divide by \(x^{2}\): \(\dfrac{3x + 2/x}{1 - 4/x^{2}} \approx 3x \to\) \(-\infty\) as \(x \to -\infty\).
A10. \(\big[2\ln(x+1) + 2\ln(x^{2}+1)\big]_{0}^{1} = 2\ln 2 + 2\ln 2 - 0 =\) \(4\ln 2 = \ln 16 \approx 2.773\). Check the second term: the derivative of \(x^{2} + 1\) is \(2x\), and the top is \(4x = 2 \cdot 2x\), so the integral is \(2\ln(x^{2}+1)\).






Study \(\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{x^{2} + 3}{x - 1}\) completely:

domain; (b) limits at the edges of the domain, and the asymptotes — vertical, horizontal or slant; (c) intersections with the axes and the sign; (d) stationary points and their nature, by the second derivative; (e) convexity and inflection; (f) range; (g) a sketch with everything above marked.



Solution to part B

(a) Domain. The denominator vanishes at \(x = 1\): \((-\infty, 1) \cup (1, +\infty)\).
(b) Limits and asymptotes. At the break: the top \(\to 4\); the bottom \(\to 0^{-}\) from the left, \(0^{+}\) from the right. So \(\lim_{x\to1^{-}} f = -\infty\), \(\lim_{x\to1^{+}} f = +\infty\): vertical asymptote \(x = 1\). At infinity: \(f \to \pm\infty\), so no horizontal asymptote. Slant: \(m = \lim \frac{f(x)}{x} = \lim \frac{x^{2}+3}{x^{2}-x} = 1\); \(b = \lim (f(x) - x) = \lim \frac{x^{2} + 3 - x^{2} + x}{x - 1} = \lim \frac{x+3}{x-1} = 1\). Slant asymptote \(y = x + 1\), at both ends.
(c) Axes and sign. \(f(0) = -3\): the curve crosses the y-axis at \((0, -3)\). \(x^{2} + 3 > 0\) always, so no zeros. The sign is the sign of \(x - 1\): negative for \(x < 1\), positive for \(x > 1\).
(d) Stationary points. \(f'(x) = \dfrac{2x(x-1) - (x^{2}+3)}{(x-1)^{2}} = \dfrac{x^{2} - 2x - 3}{(x-1)^{2}} = \dfrac{(x-3)(x+1)}{(x-1)^{2}}\), zero at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 3\). \(f''(x) = \dfrac{8}{(x-1)^{3}}\). \(f''(-1) = -1 < 0\): local maximum \((-1, -2)\). \(f''(3) = 1 > 0\): local minimum \((3, 6)\).
(e) Convexity. \(f'' < 0\) for \(x < 1\): concave; \(f'' > 0\) for \(x > 1\): convex. The sign changes only at \(x = 1\), which is outside the domain: no inflection point.
(f) Range. On the left branch the function climbs from \(-\infty\) to the maximum \(-2\) and falls back to \(-\infty\); on the right branch it falls from \(+\infty\) to the minimum \(6\) and rises again. Range \((-\infty, -2] \cup [6, +\infty)\): no value between \(-2\) and \(6\) is ever taken.
(g) Sketch. Two branches, both hugging \(y = x + 1\) far out and the line \(x = 1\) near the break; the left one a dome through \((0, -3)\) with its top at \((-1, -2)\), the right one a bowl with its bottom at \((3, 6)\). Mark both asymptotes as dashed lines.





Arno Bikes stops buying battery packs and starts assembling them in Florence, for its own bikes and for other makers. The finance office writes, in € thousand a month, with q in hundreds of packs:
\[R(q) = 48\ln(q + 1) \qquad C(q) = 0.3q^{2} + 6q + 20\]






ImportantBet before you compute



Somewhere between zero and a thousand packs a month the line makes the most money. Write down your guess, then find out.



The two schedules, seven steps each. For C and for R: domain (the algebra’s and the firm’s), limits and asymptotes, where each meets the axes, sign, maxima and minima, convexity, range. One diagram with both.
Profit, seven steps. Write π(q) and study it. How many packs a month, and what does the line earn there? Where does it break even? The equation π(q) = 0 mixes a log and a square: find both zeros by bisection, to one decimal. Sketch, with every point marked.
The cells get a duty. Of the €6k that one more hundred packs cost, €5k is lithium cells bought in Asia. The EU puts a 30% duty on them. Which term of C moves, and which do not? Rewrite C, re-solve: the new best output, the new profit, the new break-evens. Check the loss in your head first.
Board sentences. One for each of 2 and 3, in the words the founder would use.



Solution to part C

1. Cost. Domain: the algebra’s \((-\infty, +\infty)\); the firm’s \([0, +\infty)\). \(C(0) = 20\), the fixed cost: €20k a month with the line idle. \(\Delta = 36 - 24 = 12 > 0\), so the parabola has two zeros, at \(q = (-6 \pm \sqrt{12})/0.6 \approx -4.23\) and \(-15.77\) — both outside the firm’s domain; on \([0, +\infty)\) cost is always positive. The vertex, at \(q = -10\), is outside too: not the firm’s minimum. \(C'(q) = 0.6q + 6 > 0\): increasing, no max or min. \(C'' = 0.6 > 0\): convex, no inflection. \(C \to +\infty\) and \(C/q \to \infty\): no slant asymptote. Range \([20, +\infty)\).
Revenue. Domain: the algebra’s \((-1, +\infty)\); the firm’s \([0, +\infty)\). \(R(0) = 0\): through the origin, its only zero; positive after. \(R'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} > 0\): increasing. \(R''(q) = -\dfrac{48}{(q+1)^{2}} < 0\): concave — each hundred packs brings in less than the last. \(R \to +\infty\) but \(R/q \to 0\): no horizontal and no slant asymptote. Range \([0, +\infty)\).
2. Profit. \(\pi(q) = 48\ln(q+1) - 0.3q^{2} - 6q - 20\) on \([0, +\infty)\). \(\pi(0) = -20\): idle, the line loses its fixed cost. \(\pi \to -\infty\): the square beats the log. \(\pi'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} - 0.6q - 6 = 0\). Multiply by \(10(q+1)\): \(480 = (6q + 60)(q + 1)\), i.e. \(q^{2} + 11q - 70 = 0\). \(\Delta = 401\), \(\sqrt{401} \approx 20.025\), \(q^{*} = (-11 + 20.025)/2 \approx 4.51\). \(\pi''(q) = -\dfrac{48}{(q+1)^{2}} - 0.6 < 0\) everywhere: a maximum, and concave throughout, no inflection. \(\pi(4.51) \approx\) 28.75. Range \((-\infty, 28.75]\). Bisection, lower zero: \(\pi(0.6) \approx -1.15\), \(\pi(0.7) \approx +1.12\); \(\pi(0.65) \approx +0.01\) → between 0.6 and 0.65; \(\pi(0.625) \approx -0.56\) → between 0.625 and 0.65: \(q \approx 0.6\) to one decimal (exact 0.6495, just below 0.65). Upper zero: \(\pi(10) \approx 5.10\), \(\pi(11) \approx -3.02\); \(\pi(10.5) \approx 1.16\); \(\pi(10.75) \approx -0.90\); \(\pi(10.625) \approx 0.13\) → \(q \approx 10.6\) (exact 10.64). Sketch: from \((0, -20)\), up through 0.65, peak \((4.51, 28.75)\), down through 10.64.
3. The duty. \(0.30 \times 5 = 1.5\) more per hundred packs. It moves only the linear term, the cost of one more unit: \(C_{t}(q) = 0.3q^{2} + 7.5q + 20\). The square is the plant’s own cost of running harder; the fixed cost does not depend on output; revenue stays put if Arno cannot raise its price. In your head first: \(1.5 \times 4.51 \approx 6.8\) lost. \(\pi_{t}'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} - 0.6q - 7.5 = 0\) → \(480 = (6q + 75)(q + 1)\) → \(2q^{2} + 27q - 135 = 0\). \(\Delta = 1809\), \(\sqrt{1809} \approx 42.53\), \(q_{t}^{*} \approx 3.88\); \(\pi_{t}'' < 0\), a maximum. \(\pi_{t}(3.88) \approx\) 22.47: −6.28, or −22% — a little less than 6.8, because Arno makes fewer packs and stops paying the duty on the ones it drops. Break-evens: lower, \(\pi_{t}(0.6) \approx -2.05\), \(\pi_{t}(0.7) \approx +0.07\), \(\pi_{t}(0.65) \approx -0.96\) → \(q \approx 0.7\) (exact 0.696); upper, \(\pi_{t}(8.5) \approx 2.64\), \(\pi_{t}(8.75) \approx 0.72\), \(\pi_{t}(8.875) \approx -0.27\), \(\pi_{t}(8.8125) \approx 0.22\) → \(q \approx 8.8\) (exact 8.84). The profitable window shrinks from \([0.65, 10.64]\) to \([0.70, 8.84]\), mostly at the top.
4. For the founder. “Make about 450 packs a month: the line earns about €28,750 a month, and pays its way from 65 to 1,060 packs.” — “A 30% duty on the cells would cut that to 390 packs and €22,500, and above 880 packs we would lose money: worth pricing a European cell supplier now.”

Optional. This is the model of the week-3 addendum, block D: a way to organise an argument about protection, not something the midterm requires.
Arno Bikes sells e-bikes in a small country that is too small to move the world price. There, demand is Q_d = 90 − p and the country’s own makers supply Q_s = 2p − 30, with p in € hundred and Q in thousand bikes — so an area on the diagram is in € hundred thousand. Imports, Arno’s included, come in at the world price of €2,500 (p = 25).
The government, to protect its own makers, adds a tariff of €500 a bike (5).






ImportantBet before you compute



Arno loses part of its market. Does the country that imposed the tariff come out ahead?



Price and quantity if the country did not trade at all.
Free trade: bought, made at home, imported.
With the tariff: the same three. By how much do imports fall?
The consumers’ loss as an integral, the domestic makers’ gain as an integral, the tariff revenue, the protective and the consumption effects. Show that they add up, and convert the total to euro.
A Board sentence for Arno, and one for the country’s finance minister.



Solution to part E


\(90 - p = 2p - 30\) → \(p = 40\) (€4,000), \(Q = 50\) thousand bikes.
At \(p = 25\): bought 65, made at home 20, imported 45 thousand.
At \(p = 30\): bought 60, made at home 30, imported 30 thousand — imports fall by a third, 15 thousand bikes.
\(\Delta CS = \int_{25}^{30} (90 - p)\,dp = \big[90p - \tfrac{p^{2}}{2}\big]_{25}^{30} = 2250 - 1937.5 =\) 312.5. \(\Delta PS = \int_{25}^{30} (2p - 30)\,dp = \big[p^{2} - 30p\big]_{25}^{30} = 0 - (-125) =\) 125. Revenue \(= 5 \times 30 =\) 150. Protective effect \(= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (30 - 20) =\) 25; consumption effect \(= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (65 - 60) =\) 12.5. Check: \(125 + 150 + 25 + 12.5 = 312.5\) ✔. In euro: consumers lose €31.25 million; the deadweight loss is \(37.5\), €3.75 million.
For Arno: “A third of the market we shared with other importers has gone, and no price cut on our side brings it back: the tariff is on every bike.” For the minister: “The tariff moves €27.5 million from buyers to our makers and the treasury, and €3.75 million simply disappears — that is the price of protection, and it does not count retaliation.”

\[R(q) = 48\ln(q + 1) \qquad C(q) = 0.3q^{2} + 6q + 20\]






ImportantBet before you compute



Somewhere between zero and a thousand packs a month the line makes the most money. Write down your guess, then find out.



The two schedules, seven steps each. For C and for R: domain (the algebra’s and the firm’s), limits and asymptotes, where each meets the axes, sign, maxima and minima, convexity, range. One diagram with both.
Profit, seven steps. Write π(q) and study it. How many packs a month, and what does the line earn there? Where does it break even? The equation π(q) = 0 mixes a log and a square: find both zeros by bisection, to one decimal. Sketch, with every point marked.
The cells get a duty. Of the €6k that one more hundred packs cost, €5k is lithium cells bought in Asia. The EU puts a 30% duty on them. Which term of C moves, and which do not? Rewrite C, re-solve: the new best output, the new profit, the new break-evens. Check the loss in your head first.
Board sentences. One for each of 2 and 3, in the words the founder would use.



Solution to part C

1. Cost. Domain: the algebra’s \((-\infty, +\infty)\); the firm’s \([0, +\infty)\). \(C(0) = 20\), the fixed cost: €20k a month with the line idle. \(\Delta = 36 - 24 = 12 > 0\), so the parabola has two zeros, at \(q = (-6 \pm \sqrt{12})/0.6 \approx -4.23\) and \(-15.77\) — both outside the firm’s domain; on \([0, +\infty)\) cost is always positive. The vertex, at \(q = -10\), is outside too: not the firm’s minimum. \(C'(q) = 0.6q + 6 > 0\): increasing, no max or min. \(C'' = 0.6 > 0\): convex, no inflection. \(C \to +\infty\) and \(C/q \to \infty\): no slant asymptote. Range \([20, +\infty)\).
Revenue. Domain: the algebra’s \((-1, +\infty)\); the firm’s \([0, +\infty)\). \(R(0) = 0\): through the origin, its only zero; positive after. \(R'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} > 0\): increasing. \(R''(q) = -\dfrac{48}{(q+1)^{2}} < 0\): concave — each hundred packs brings in less than the last. \(R \to +\infty\) but \(R/q \to 0\): no horizontal and no slant asymptote. Range \([0, +\infty)\).
2. Profit. \(\pi(q) = 48\ln(q+1) - 0.3q^{2} - 6q - 20\) on \([0, +\infty)\). \(\pi(0) = -20\): idle, the line loses its fixed cost. \(\pi \to -\infty\): the square beats the log. \(\pi'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} - 0.6q - 6 = 0\). Multiply by \(10(q+1)\): \(480 = (6q + 60)(q + 1)\), i.e. \(q^{2} + 11q - 70 = 0\). \(\Delta = 401\), \(\sqrt{401} \approx 20.025\), \(q^{*} = (-11 + 20.025)/2 \approx 4.51\). \(\pi''(q) = -\dfrac{48}{(q+1)^{2}} - 0.6 < 0\) everywhere: a maximum, and concave throughout, no inflection. \(\pi(4.51) \approx\) 28.75. Range \((-\infty, 28.75]\). Bisection, lower zero: \(\pi(0.6) \approx -1.15\), \(\pi(0.7) \approx +1.12\); \(\pi(0.65) \approx +0.01\) → between 0.6 and 0.65; \(\pi(0.625) \approx -0.56\) → between 0.625 and 0.65: \(q \approx 0.6\) to one decimal (exact 0.6495, just below 0.65). Upper zero: \(\pi(10) \approx 5.10\), \(\pi(11) \approx -3.02\); \(\pi(10.5) \approx 1.16\); \(\pi(10.75) \approx -0.90\); \(\pi(10.625) \approx 0.13\) → \(q \approx 10.6\) (exact 10.64). Sketch: from \((0, -20)\), up through 0.65, peak \((4.51, 28.75)\), down through 10.64.
3. The duty. \(0.30 \times 5 = 1.5\) more per hundred packs. It moves only the linear term, the cost of one more unit: \(C_{t}(q) = 0.3q^{2} + 7.5q + 20\). The square is the plant’s own cost of running harder; the fixed cost does not depend on output; revenue stays put if Arno cannot raise its price. In your head first: \(1.5 \times 4.51 \approx 6.8\) lost. \(\pi_{t}'(q) = \dfrac{48}{q+1} - 0.6q - 7.5 = 0\) → \(480 = (6q + 75)(q + 1)\) → \(2q^{2} + 27q - 135 = 0\). \(\Delta = 1809\), \(\sqrt{1809} \approx 42.53\), \(q_{t}^{*} \approx 3.88\); \(\pi_{t}'' < 0\), a maximum. \(\pi_{t}(3.88) \approx\) 22.47: −6.28, or −22% — a little less than 6.8, because Arno makes fewer packs and stops paying the duty on the ones it drops. Break-evens: lower, \(\pi_{t}(0.6) \approx -2.05\), \(\pi_{t}(0.7) \approx +0.07\), \(\pi_{t}(0.65) \approx -0.96\) → \(q \approx 0.7\) (exact 0.696); upper, \(\pi_{t}(8.5) \approx 2.64\), \(\pi_{t}(8.75) \approx 0.72\), \(\pi_{t}(8.875) \approx -0.27\), \(\pi_{t}(8.8125) \approx 0.22\) → \(q \approx 8.8\) (exact 8.84). The profitable window shrinks from \([0.65, 10.64]\) to \([0.70, 8.84]\), mostly at the top.
4. For the founder. “Make about 450 packs a month: the line earns about €28,750 a month, and pays its way from 65 to 1,060 packs.” — “A 30% duty on the cells would cut that to 390 packs and €22,500, and above 880 packs we would lose money: worth pricing a European cell supplier now.”

title: Reading week — The full mock: weeks 1–5 in one sitting
text:
Optional. This is the model of the week-3 addendum, block D: a way to organise an argument about protection, not something the midterm requires.
Arno Bikes sells e-bikes in a small country that is too small to move the world price. There, demand is Q_d = 90 − p and the country’s own makers supply Q_s = 2p − 30, with p in € hundred and Q in thousand bikes — so an area on the diagram is in € hundred thousand. Imports, Arno’s included, come in at the world price of €2,500 (p = 25).
The government, to protect its own makers, adds a tariff of €500 a bike (5).






ImportantBet before you compute



Arno loses part of its market. Does the country that imposed the tariff come out ahead?



Price and quantity if the country did not trade at all.
Free trade: bought, made at home, imported.
With the tariff: the same three. By how much do imports fall?
The consumers’ loss as an integral, the domestic makers’ gain as an integral, the tariff revenue, the protective and the consumption effects. Show that they add up, and convert the total to euro.
A Board sentence for Arno, and one for the country’s finance minister.



Solution to part E


\(90 - p = 2p - 30\) → \(p = 40\) (€4,000), \(Q = 50\) thousand bikes.
At \(p = 25\): bought 65, made at home 20, imported 45 thousand.
At \(p = 30\): bought 60, made at home 30, imported 30 thousand — imports fall by a third, 15 thousand bikes.
\(\Delta CS = \int_{25}^{30} (90 - p)\,dp = \big[90p - \tfrac{p^{2}}{2}\big]_{25}^{30} = 2250 - 1937.5 =\) 312.5. \(\Delta PS = \int_{25}^{30} (2p - 30)\,dp = \big[p^{2} - 30p\big]_{25}^{30} = 0 - (-125) =\) 125. Revenue \(= 5 \times 30 =\) 150. Protective effect \(= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (30 - 20) =\) 25; consumption effect \(= \tfrac12 \times 5 \times (65 - 60) =\) 12.5. Check: \(125 + 150 + 25 + 12.5 = 312.5\) ✔. In euro: consumers lose €31.25 million; the deadweight loss is \(37.5\), €3.75 million.
For Arno: “A third of the market we shared with other importers has gone, and no price cut on our side brings it back: the tariff is on every bike.” For the minister: “The tariff moves €27.5 million from buyers to our makers and the treasury, and €3.75 million simply disappears — that is the price of protection, and it does not count retaliation.”

title: Week 5 — Drills
text:
Exam format. Show all work. Core items are for everyone; stretch items for whoever finishes early. Solutions at the end, worked the way an examiner wants to see them.
Running case: Arno Bikes holds a small bond portfolio as a cash reserve, and is asked by the Board whether rising rates should worry it.
Unless stated otherwise: annual coupons, face value €100, prices to the cent.


D1 (core). A 5-year bond, 4% annual coupon, face €100, yield 6%. (a) Write the price as a sum. (b) Compute it. (c) Is it at a premium or a discount, and why — in one sentence, without arithmetic?
D2 (core). The same bond at a yield of 4%. Then at 2%. (a) Both prices. (b) State the rule that connects coupon, yield and price.
D3 (core — resit form). Select the correct alternative and justify in one line. A bond trades above par. Therefore: (i) its coupon is above its yield (ii) its yield is above its coupon (iii) it must be close to maturity
D4 (core). A zero-coupon bond pays €100 in 8 years. The yield is 5%. (a) Its price today. (b) If the yield rises to 6%, the new price and the percentage change.



D5 (core). For the 5-year 4% bond priced at a 6% yield (D1): (a) Compute Macaulay duration, showing the weight of each cash flow. (b) Convert it to modified duration. (c) Estimate the price change if the yield rises by 50 basis points.
D6 (core). A 10-year bond with a 5% coupon trades at par (yield 5%). Its modified duration is 7.72. (a) Estimate the new price if the yield rises to 6%. (b) The actual price at 6% is €92.64. Compare, and say which way the estimate errs.
D7 (stretch). Without computing anything, order these three by duration, longest first, and justify each comparison in one clause: (i) a 10-year zero-coupon bond (ii) a 10-year 8% coupon bond (iii) a 3-year 8% coupon bond



D8 (core). Using the bond in D6 (P = 100, D_mod = 7.72, convexity C = 75.0): (a) Estimate the price at a yield of 6% using duration and convexity. (b) Compare with the actual €92.64 and with the duration-only estimate from D6.
D9 (core — the Board sentence). In two sentences, no formulas: what does convexity buy the holder of a bond, and why does a risk manager care about it?
D10 (stretch). Two bonds have the same duration; one has higher convexity. Rates move sharply, direction unknown. Which would you rather hold, and why?
The session closes with a mock of the final exam’s calculus question, thirty minutes in exam conditions.



D11 (core). Arno Bikes holds €400,000 of the D6 bond (at par) and €600,000 of a 2-year bond with modified duration 1.90. (a) The portfolio’s modified duration. (Weight each by market value.) (b) The estimated loss in euros if yields rise by 1% across the board. (c) One sentence to the Board.



The step after duration: using it to make a payment safe. A zero’s Macaulay duration is its maturity; yields are flat and move once, the day after purchase.
D12 (core). Arno Bikes must pay a supplier €500,000 in exactly 3 years. It can buy 1-year and 5-year zero-coupon bonds, both yielding 4%. (a) How much must it set aside today? (b) What share goes into each zero so that the portfolio’s duration is 3 years? (c) The euros in each, and the amount each zero pays at maturity.
D13 (core). The day after the purchase in D12, yields jump to 5% and stay there. (a) The 1-year zero’s payment, reinvested at 5% until year 3: what is it worth then? (b) The 5-year zero, still two years from maturity at year 3: what is it worth then? (c) The total against the €500,000 owed. Then repeat (a)–(c) with yields falling to 3% instead, and say what you notice.
D14 (stretch). Go back to the slide: €1M due in 4 years, flat yield 5%, money set aside today €822,702.47. Replace the 6-year zero with a 6-year 5% coupon bond at par. (a) Its Macaulay duration, with the table of weights. (b) The share in the 2-year zero that makes the portfolio’s duration 4 years, and the euros in each. (c) One year later, yields unchanged: the payment is 3 years away, and the coupon bond is now a 5-year 5% bond at par, with Macaulay duration 4.55. By how much did each duration fall? What must the treasurer do, and how often?

D2. (a) At 4%: coupon equals yield, so P = **€100.00** (par). At 2%: 4 × [1 − (1.02)⁻⁵]/0.02 + 100/(1.02)⁵ = 4 × 4.713460 + 90.573 = 18.854 + 90.573 = **€109.43**. (b) Coupon > yield → premium; coupon = yield → par; coupon < yield → discount. Price and yield move in opposite directions, always.
D3. (i) its coupon is above its yield. Investors pay more than face only to obtain a coupon better than the going rate.

(b) D_mod = D/(1 + y) = 4.611/1.06 = **4.350**. (c) ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod × Δy = −4.350 × 0.005 = −2.18%, i.e. about −€1.99, giving roughly €89.59.
D6. (a) ΔP/P ≈ −7.72 × 0.01 = −7.72% → P ≈ 100 × 0.9228 = **€92.28**. (b) The actual price is €92.64, so the estimate is €0.36 too low. Duration alone overstates the loss. It will also understate the gain when yields fall: the straight line lies below the curve on both sides.
D7. (i) > (ii) > (iii). (i) beats (ii): a zero pays everything at the end, so its weighted average time is the full 10 years, while coupons pull (ii)’s average forward. (ii) beats (iii): same coupon, but money returned over ten years instead of three.
D8. (a) ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod Δy + ½ C (Δy)² = −7.72(0.01) + ½(75.0)(0.0001) = −0.0772 + 0.00375 = −0.07345 → P ≈ 100 × 0.92655 = **€92.66**. (b) Duration alone gave €92.28, out by 36 cents below the truth. Adding convexity gives €92.66, out by 2 cents above it. The second term recovers almost all of the curvature the straight line missed; the 2 cents that remain belong to the next term again, and no one on a trading floor cares about them.
D9. Convexity means the price curve bends away from the straight-line estimate in the holder’s favour: when yields fall the bond gains more than duration predicts, and when they rise it loses less. A risk manager cares because a duration-only report overstates losses and understates gains, and because between two bonds of equal duration the more convex one is worth more when rates move a long way.
D10. The more convex one. With equal duration the two behave the same for a small move, but for a large move in either direction the convex bond does better: more upside, less downside. That asymmetry is worth paying for, and in the market you usually do.

Half in each. (c) €222,249.09 in each. The 1-year zero pays 222,249.09 × 1.04 = **€231,139.05** in year 1. The 5-year zero pays 222,249.09 × (1.04)⁵ = **€270,400.00** in year 5.

(c) One year later, yields unchanged: the payment is 3 years away, and the coupon bond is now a 5-year 5% bond at par, with Macaulay duration 4.55. By how much did each duration fall? What must the treasurer do, and how often?



Solutions

D1. (a) P = Σ(t=1..5) 4/(1.06)^t + 100/(1.06)^5. (b) Annuity part: 4 × [1 − (1.06)⁻⁵]/0.06 = 4 × 4.212364 = 16.85. Face: 100/(1.06)⁵ = 74.73. P = **€91.58**. (c) A discount: the bond pays 4% on its face while the market demands 6%, so it must be cheaper than face to make up the difference.
D2. (a) At 4%: coupon equals yield, so P = **€100.00** (par). At 2%: 4 × [1 − (1.02)⁻⁵]/0.02 + 100/(1.02)⁵ = 4 × 4.713460 + 90.573 = 18.854 + 90.573 = **€109.43**. (b) Coupon > yield → premium; coupon = yield → par; coupon < yield → discount. Price and yield move in opposite directions, always.
D3. (i) its coupon is above its yield. Investors pay more than face only to obtain a coupon better than the going rate.
D4. (a) P = 100/(1.05)⁸ = 100/1.477455 = **€67.68**. (b) P = 100/(1.06)⁸ = 100/1.593848 = **€62.74**; change = (62.74 − 67.68)/67.68 = **−7.30%**.

(b) D_mod = D/(1 + y) = 4.611/1.06 = **4.350**. (c) ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod × Δy = −4.350 × 0.005 = −2.18%, i.e. about −€1.99, giving roughly €89.59.
D6. (a) ΔP/P ≈ −7.72 × 0.01 = −7.72% → P ≈ 100 × 0.9228 = **€92.28**. (b) The actual price is €92.64, so the estimate is €0.36 too low. Duration alone overstates the loss. It will also understate the gain when yields fall: the straight line lies below the curve on both sides.
D7. (i) > (ii) > (iii). (i) beats (ii): a zero pays everything at the end, so its weighted average time is the full 10 years, while coupons pull (ii)’s average forward. (ii) beats (iii): same coupon, but money returned over ten years instead of three.
D8. (a) ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod Δy + ½ C (Δy)² = −7.72(0.01) + ½(75.0)(0.0001) = −0.0772 + 0.00375 = −0.07345 → P ≈ 100 × 0.92655 = **€92.66**. (b) Duration alone gave €92.28, out by 36 cents below the truth. Adding convexity gives €92.66, out by 2 cents above it. The second term recovers almost all of the curvature the straight line missed; the 2 cents that remain belong to the next term again, and no one on a trading floor cares about them.
D9. Convexity means the price curve bends away from the straight-line estimate in the holder’s favour: when yields fall the bond gains more than duration predicts, and when they rise it loses less. A risk manager cares because a duration-only report overstates losses and understates gains, and because between two bonds of equal duration the more convex one is worth more when rates move a long way.
D10. The more convex one. With equal duration the two behave the same for a small move, but for a large move in either direction the convex bond does better: more upside, less downside. That asymmetry is worth paying for, and in the market you usually do.
D11. (a) Weights 400/1,000 = 0.4 and 600/1,000 = 0.6. D_portfolio = 0.4(7.72) + 0.6(1.90) = 3.088 + 1.140 = **4.228**. (b) ΔV ≈ −4.228 × 0.01 × €1,000,000 = **−€42,280**. (c) “A one-point rise in yields costs the reserve about €42,000, a little over 4% of it; about three quarters of the exposure sits in the ten-year holding, and shortening that would cut it roughly in half.”
D12. (a) PV = 500,000/(1.04)³ = 500,000/1.124864 = **€444,498.18**. (b) Each zero’s duration is its maturity. With a share w in the 1-year zero: 1·w + 5(1 − w) = 3 → 5 − 4w = 3 → **w = ½**. Half in each. (c) €222,249.09 in each. The 1-year zero pays 222,249.09 × 1.04 = **€231,139.05** in year 1. The 5-year zero pays 222,249.09 × (1.04)⁵ = **€270,400.00** in year 5.
D13. (a) 231,139.05 × (1.05)² = 231,139.05 × 1.1025 = **€254,830.80**. (b) 270,400.00/(1.05)² = 270,400.00/1.1025 = **€245,260.77**. (c) 254,830.80 + 245,260.77 = **€500,091.57**, i.e. €91.57 more than the €500,000 owed. At 3%: 231,139.05 × 1.0609 = 245,215.42 and 270,400.00/1.0609 = 254,877.93, total €500,093.35, €93.35 more. In both directions the reinvestment effect and the price effect cancel, and what is left over is a small gain: that is convexity, on the holder’s side again. Without the match — all in the 1-year zero — a fall to 3% would leave 444,498.18 × 1.04 × 1.0609 = €490,430.84, about €9,570 short.
