title: Week 3 — Drills
text:
Exam format. Show all work. Core items are for everyone; stretch items for whoever finishes early. Solutions at the end, worked the way an examiner wants to see them.
The seven-point study, in the order the midterm expects it: domain → zeros → sign → stationary points → nature (max/min) → shape (convexity, inflection) → sketch.


D1 (core — the midterm rehearsal). Study π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000 completely and sketch it. Give: domain, zeros, sign line, π' and the stationary point, π'' and its nature, behaviour as q → ∞, and a labelled sketch.
D2 (core). A cost function: C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25 (€ thousand), for q ≥ 0. (a) Domain, and C(0). What is C(0) called? (b) Average cost AC(q) = C(q)/q. Find its domain and lim (q→0⁺) AC(q) and lim (q→∞) AC(q). (c) Minimise AC(q). At that quantity, compute AC and C'(q) and comment on what you notice.
D2b (core — asymptotes, in the resit’s own form). f(x) = x² − 3x + 7 ln(x + 3). (a) State the domain as an interval. (b) Evaluate lim (x→−3⁺) f(x) and say what it tells you about the graph. (c) Evaluate lim (x→+∞) f(x). (d) Sketch the shape, marking the asymptote.
D3 (stretch). f(q) = q³ − 12q² + 36q on [0, 10]. (a) Stationary points and their nature. (b) Inflection point. (c) Sketch.
D3b (core — step 6 on its own). f(q) = q³ − 6q² + 9q + 4, for q ≥ 0. (a) Compute f''(q) and solve f''(q) = 0. (b) Give the sign of f'' on each side of that point and name the intervals: convex where, concave where. (c) The inflection point, with both coordinates. (d) The stationary points, and the nature of each one — using f'', not a sketch. (e) One sentence a report would use for step 6.



D4 (core). A second firm: R(q) = 30 ln(q + 1), C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25, both in € thousand, q ≥ 0. (a) Write π(q). (b) Write π'(q). (c) Solve π'(q) = 0. Leave it as an equation in q first, then solve the quadratic it becomes. (d) Confirm with π'' that it is a maximum. (e) Is the firm profitable at that quantity? Answer with a number.
D5 (core — the managerial reading). For the firm in D4, R'(q) is marginal revenue and C'(q) is marginal cost. (a) Write the condition π'(q) = 0 as R'(q) = C'(q), in words. (b) At q = 2 compute both. Which is larger, and what should the firm do?
D6 (stretch). A box with a square base and no lid must hold 32 m³. Minimise the material used. (Surface S = x² + 4xh, volume x²h = 32.)



D7 (core — exam form). Evaluate, splitting term by term: (a) ∫ (q⁵ − 3q³ + 2)/q² dq (b) ∫ (4q³ − 6q + 5) dq (c) ∫ (2/q + 3√q) dq
D8 (core — exam form). Find f(q) given f'(q) = 12q² − 6q + 1 and f(2) = 20.
D8b (core — exam form, and the one that catches people). Find f(x) given f'(x) = 12x² − 4x and f(−3) = 17. Watch every sign.
D8c (core — the third rule). Evaluate, by asking first whether the top is the derivative of the bottom: (a) ∫ 1/(q − 4) dq (b) ∫ q/(q² + 5) dq (c) ∫ (2q + 3)/(q² + 3q − 1) dq (d) ∫ 5/(2q + 1) dq
D9 (core). Evaluate the definite integrals and say what each measures: (a) ∫₀²⁰ (0.8q + 3) dq where 0.8q + 3 is marginal cost. (b) ∫₁⁴ (6/q) dq. Leave the answer in terms of ln.
D9b (core — exam form). Evaluate ∫₀^(1/2) [ 1/(x − 1) + x/(x² − 1) ] dx, leaving the answer in terms of ln. Both terms are logs; neither is 1/x.
D10 (stretch). Marginal profit is π'(q) = 1200 − 8q. The firm currently makes 100 bikes. (a) By how much does profit change if output rises from 100 to 150? Compute it as a definite integral. (b) Check your answer against π(150) − π(100) using π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000.



Added on 22 October, not covered in class: self-study for the midterm, with the addendum at the end of the week-3 slides.
D11 (core — the brief’s tariff question, different numbers). A firm has R(q) = 60 ln(q + 1) and C(q) = 0.25q² + 5q + 30, € thousand, q ≥ 0. Of the €5k that one more unit costs, €4k is a component imported from outside the EU. The EU imposes a 20% tariff on it. (a) Say which term of C the tariff moves, which it leaves alone, and why. Write the new cost C_t(q). (b) Find the profit-maximising output before and after the tariff. Confirm each is a maximum with π''. (c) Profit at each optimum, and the change in euro and in percent. (d) Check (c) in your head: tariff per unit × output. Why is the exact loss a little smaller? (e) One sentence for the Board.
D12 (core — a zero by bisection). For the firm of D11 with the tariff, π_t(q) = 60 ln(q + 1) − 0.25q² − 5.8q − 30. (a) Show that π_t changes sign between q = 0.75 and q = 0.8, and between q = 14 and q = 14.5. (b) Halve each interval until you can state both break-even outputs to one decimal place. (c) Before the tariff the break-evens were 0.76 and 15.57. What happened to the profitable window?
D13 (optional — the small-nation model). A small open economy: demand Q_d = 120 − 2p, domestic supply Q_s = 3p − 30 (Q in thousand units, p in €). The world price is €20. (a) Price and quantity with no trade (autarky). (b) Under free trade: quantity bought, made at home, imported. (c) A tariff of €5 a unit. The same three quantities. (d) Compute, as integrals or as areas: the loss of consumer surplus, the gain of domestic producers, the tariff revenue, and the two triangles — the protective and the consumption effect. Check that they add up. (e) What is the deadweight loss, and what does it mean in one sentence?
D14 (stretch — writing). In 150–200 words for a Board, explain why a tariff hurts a small open economy more than the triangles of D13 suggest. Find the channels yourself, and support each with a source you have actually read.



Solutions

D1. - Domain. A polynomial: all of ℝ. For a quantity, [0, +∞). - Zeros. −4q² + 1200q − 60,000 = 0; divide by −4: q² − 300q + 15,000 = 0. Δ = 90,000 − 60,000 = 30,000, √Δ ≈ 173.2. q = (300 ± 173.2)/2 → q ≈ 63.4 and q ≈ 236.6. - Sign. a = −4 < 0, so positive between the roots: π > 0 on (63.4, 236.6), negative outside. - Stationary point. π'(q) = −8q + 1200 = 0 → q = 150. - Nature. π''(q) = −8 < 0 for every q, so the stationary point is a maximum; the curve is concave everywhere. π(150) = −90,000 + 180,000 − 60,000 = **€30,000**. - Behaviour. lim (q→∞) π(q) = −∞: the −4q² term wins. There is no “sell more forever”. - Sketch. Downward parabola, crossing the axis at 63.4 and 236.6, peak (150, 30,000), intercept π(0) = −60,000. Label all four.
D2. (a) [0, +∞); C(0) = 25. That is fixed cost: what the firm pays having produced nothing. (b) AC(q) = 0.4q + 3 + 25/q, domain (0, +∞) — zero output has no average. lim (q→0⁺) AC = +∞ (fixed cost spread over almost nothing). lim (q→∞) AC = +∞ (the 0.4q term takes over). So AC falls, then rises: it has a minimum. (c) AC'(q) = 0.4 − 25/q² = 0 → q² = 62.5 → q ≈ 7.91. AC(7.91) = 3.16 + 3 + 3.16 = **9.32**; C'(7.91) = 0.8(7.91) + 3 = **9.32**. They are equal. Average cost is at its lowest exactly where marginal cost crosses it. Worth stating out loud: it is not a coincidence, it is what “average” means.
D2b. (a) ln(x + 3) needs x + 3 > 0, so the domain is (−3, +∞) — open, because ln 0 is undefined. (b) As x → −3⁺, ln(x+3) → −∞, and x² − 3x → 18, so f(x) → **−∞**. The line x = −3 is a vertical asymptote: the curve plunges down it. (c) As x → +∞ the x² term dominates everything, so f(x) → **+∞**. (d) f'(x) = 2x − 3 + 7/(x + 3) = (2x − 1)(x + 2)/(x + 3), zero at x = −2 and x = ½. So the curve comes up from −∞ along x = −3, reaches a local maximum at (−2, 10), dips to a local minimum at (½, ≈ 7.52), then rises to +∞. Two turns, not one. Draw the asymptote as a dashed vertical line: the marker looks for it.
D3. (a) f'(q) = 3q² − 24q + 36 = 3(q² − 8q + 12) = 3(q − 2)(q − 6) → q = 2, 6. f''(q) = 6q − 24: f''(2) = −12 < 0 → maximum, f(2) = 8 − 48 + 72 = 32. f''(6) = 12 > 0 → minimum, f(6) = 216 − 432 + 216 = 0. (b) f'' = 0 at q = 4, f(4) = 64 − 192 + 144 = 16; the curvature changes sign there, so it is an inflection. (c) Rises to (2, 32), falls to (6, 0), rises again; at q = 10, f = 1000 − 1200 + 360 = 160.
D3b. (a) f'(q) = 3q² − 12q + 9, f''(q) = 6q − 12. f'' = 0 at q = 2. (b) f''(1) = −6 < 0: concave on [0, 2). f''(3) = 6 > 0: convex on (2, ∞). The sign changes, so q = 2 is a genuine inflection and not just a zero. (c) f(2) = 8 − 24 + 18 + 4 = 6: inflection at (2, 6). Both coordinates, or the point is not located. (d) f'(q) = 3(q − 1)(q − 3) = 0 → q = 1, 3. f''(1) = −6 < 0 → maximum, f(1) = 8. f''(3) = 6 > 0 → minimum, f(3) = 4. Max at 1, inflection at 2, min at 3: the inflection sits between the turning points, where the fall is steepest. (e) “The curve is concave up to q = 2 and convex beyond it, with an inflection at (2, 6): the decline that begins at the maximum is steepest there, and slows afterwards until the minimum at q = 3.”
D4. (a) π(q) = 30 ln(q + 1) − 0.4q² − 3q − 25. (b) π'(q) = 30/(q + 1) − 0.8q − 3. (c) 30/(q + 1) = 0.8q + 3. Multiply by (q + 1): 30 = (0.8q + 3)(q + 1) = 0.8q² + 3.8q + 3 → 0.8q² + 3.8q − 27 = 0. Multiply by 5: 4q² + 19q − 135 = 0. Δ = 361 + 2160 = 2521, √Δ ≈ 50.21. q = (−19 ± 50.21)/8 → q ≈ 3.90 (the negative root is discarded: a quantity). (d) π''(q) = −30/(q + 1)² − 0.8 < 0 everywhere → maximum. (e) π(3.90) = 30 ln(4.90) − 0.4(15.21) − 3(3.90) − 25 = 47.68 − 6.08 − 11.70 − 25 = **€4.89k**. Profitable, but only just — the window is narrow, which is the point.
D5. (a) π' = R' − C' = 0 means R'(q) = C'(q): produce up to the point where the revenue from one more unit equals what that unit costs. (b) R'(2) = 30/3 = **10**; C'(2) = 0.8(2) + 3 = **4.6**. Marginal revenue is larger, so each extra unit still adds 10 − 4.6 = 5.4 — produce more, up to q ≈ 3.90.
D6. h = 32/x², so S = x² + 4x(32/x²) = x² + 128/x. S' = 2x − 128/x² = 0 → x³ = 64 → x = 4, h = 2. S'' = 2 + 256/x³ > 0 → minimum. S = 16 + 32 = **48 m²**.
D7. (a) Split first: (q⁵ − 3q³ + 2)/q² = q³ − 3q + 2q⁻². ∫ = q⁴/4 − 3q²/2 − 2/q + c. (b) q⁴ − 3q² + 5q + c. (c) ∫ 2/q dq = 2 ln|q|; ∫ 3q^{1/2} dq = 3 · (2/3) q^{3/2} = 2q^{3/2}. Total: 2 ln|q| + 2q^{3/2} + c. The exam’s integral is always this shape: divide term by term first, then each term is a power or a log.
D8. f(q) = 4q³ − 3q² + q + c. f(2) = 32 − 12 + 2 + c = 20 → c = −2. f(q) = 4q³ − 3q² + q − 2.
D8b. f(x) = 4x³ − 2x² + c. Now substitute carefully: f(−3) = 4(−27) − 2(9) + c = −108 − 18 + c = −126 + c = 17 → c = 143. f(x) = 4x³ − 2x² + 143. The trap is (−3)³ = −27 and (−3)² = +9. Two signs, two marks.
D8c. Ask each time: is the top the derivative of the bottom? (a) bottom differentiates to 1 → ln|q − 4| + c. (b) bottom differentiates to 2q, top is q, so a factor ½ is missing → ½ ln(q² + 5) + c. (No modulus needed: q² + 5 > 0 always.) (c) bottom differentiates to 2q + 3, which is exactly the top → ln|q² + 3q − 1| + c. (d) bottom differentiates to 2, top is 5, so 5/2 comes out → (5/2) ln|2q + 1| + c.
D9. (a) [0.4q² + 3q]₀²⁰ = 160 + 60 = **220**. Total variable cost of the first 20 bikes: adding up marginal cost gives total cost. (b) [6 ln q]₁⁴ = 6 ln 4 − 6 ln 1 = **6 ln 4 ≈ 8.32**.
D9b. Each term is a log. ∫ 1/(x−1) dx = ln|x−1|; ∫ x/(x²−1) dx = ½ ln|x²−1|. So the antiderivative is ln|x−1| + ½ ln|x²−1|, and
at ½ :  ln(½) + ½ ln(¾) = −0.6931 + ½(−0.2877) = −0.8370 at 0 :  ln 1 + ½ ln 1 = 0
= −0.8370, or exactly ln(½) + ½ ln(¾). Note the modulus: between 0 and ½ both x − 1 and x² − 1 are negative, and without the absolute value the logs are undefined. The exam’s model answer expects it.
D10. (a) ∫₁₀₀¹⁵⁰ (1200 − 8q) dq = [1200q − 4q²]₁₀₀¹⁵⁰ = (180,000 − 90,000) − (120,000 − 40,000) = 90,000 − 80,000 = **€10,000**. (b) π(150) = 30,000; π(100) = −40,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 = 20,000. Difference = **€10,000**. ✔ The integral of the marginal is the change in the total. That sentence is the whole of integration.
D11. (a) The tariff raises what the firm pays per unit for the component: 4 × 0.20 = €0.8k more per unit. That is the linear term, 5q → 5.8q. The quadratic term 0.25q² is the plant’s internal cost of running harder (overtime, congestion), not a purchase: untouched. The fixed cost 30 does not depend on output: untouched. C_t(q) = 0.25q² + 5.8q + 30. Revenue unchanged, assuming the firm cannot raise its price. (b) Before: π'(q) = 60/(q + 1) − 0.5q − 5 = 0 → 60 = (0.5q + 5)(q + 1) = 0.5q² + 5.5q + 5 → q² + 11q − 110 = 0. Δ = 121 + 440 = 561, √Δ ≈ 23.685, q* = (−11 + 23.685)/2 ≈ 6.34 (the negative root is outside the domain). After: 60 = (0.5q + 5.8)(q + 1) = 0.5q² + 6.3q + 5.8 → q² + 12.6q − 108.4 = 0. Δ = 158.76 + 433.6 = 592.36, √Δ ≈ 24.339, q_t* = (−12.6 + 24.339)/2 ≈ 5.87. Both: π''(q) = −60/(q + 1)² − 0.5 < 0 for every q ≥ 0, so each is a maximum (≈ −1.61 and −1.77). (c) π(6.34) = 60 ln 7.34 − 0.25(6.34)² − 5(6.34) − 30 ≈ **47.85**; π_t(5.87) ≈ **42.97**. Change −€4.88k, −10.2%. (d) 0.8 × 6.34 ≈ 5.07. The exact loss is smaller because the firm cuts output by half a unit and stops paying the tariff on what it no longer makes. (e) “The tariff costs us about €4.9k a month, a tenth of our profit; we should produce about 5.9 units instead of 6.3.”
D12. (a) π_t(0.75) ≈ −0.91, π_t(0.8) ≈ +0.47; π_t(14) ≈ +2.28, π_t(14.5) ≈ −2.21. Each pair has opposite signs, so π_t crosses zero inside each interval (it is continuous there). (b) Lower: π_t(0.775) ≈ −0.22 → between 0.775 and 0.8; π_t(0.7875) ≈ +0.13 → between 0.775 and 0.7875. Every number in there rounds to q ≈ 0.8 (exact 0.783). Upper: π_t(14.25) ≈ +0.06 → between 14.25 and 14.5; π_t(14.3) ≈ −0.39 → between 14.25 and 14.3: q ≈ 14.3 (exact 14.257). (c) From [0.76, 15.57] to [0.78, 14.26]: the window shrinks, mostly at the top. At high output the tariff is paid on many units, so the firm stops covering its costs much sooner.
D13. (a) 120 − 2p = 3p − 30 → p = 30, Q = 60. (b) At p = 20: bought Q_d = 80, made at home Q_s = 30, imported 50. (c) At p = 25: bought 70, made at home 45, imported 25. (d) ΔCS = ∫₂₀²⁵ (120 − 2p) dp = [120p − p²]₂₀²⁵ = 2375 − 2000 = **375**. ΔPS = ∫₂₀²⁵ (3p − 30) dp = [1.5p² − 30p]₂₀²⁵ = 187.5 − 0 = **187.5**. Revenue = 5 × 25 = **125**. Protective effect = ½ × 5 × (45 − 30) = **37.5**; consumption effect = ½ × 5 × (80 − 70) = **25**. Check: 187.5 + 125 + 37.5 + 25 = 375 ✔ (all in € thousand). (e) Deadweight loss = 37.5 + 25 = **62.5**: the part of the consumers’ loss that nobody gains — production done at home at more than the world price, and purchases that no longer happen.
D14. No model answer, on purpose: finding and judging the sources is the exercise. Check your paragraph against the method: each channel named precisely, a recent and reliable source cited Harvard, the way it reaches a firm’s costs or revenue, the direction, and what a Board should do. At least one channel should come back to the cost function of D11. Wikipedia is not a source.

title: Week 3 — Drills
text:
D1 (core — the midterm rehearsal). Study π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000 completely and sketch it. Give: domain, zeros, sign line, π' and the stationary point, π'' and its nature, behaviour as q → ∞, and a labelled sketch.
D2 (core). A cost function: C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25 (€ thousand), for q ≥ 0. (a) Domain, and C(0). What is C(0) called? (b) Average cost AC(q) = C(q)/q. Find its domain and lim (q→0⁺) AC(q) and lim (q→∞) AC(q). (c) Minimise AC(q). At that quantity, compute AC and C'(q) and comment on what you notice.
D2b (core — asymptotes, in the resit’s own form). f(x) = x² − 3x + 7 ln(x + 3). (a) State the domain as an interval. (b) Evaluate lim (x→−3⁺) f(x) and say what it tells you about the graph. (c) Evaluate lim (x→+∞) f(x). (d) Sketch the shape, marking the asymptote.
D3 (stretch). f(q) = q³ − 12q² + 36q on [0, 10]. (a) Stationary points and their nature. (b) Inflection point. (c) Sketch.
D3b (core — step 6 on its own). f(q) = q³ − 6q² + 9q + 4, for q ≥ 0. (a) Compute f''(q) and solve f''(q) = 0. (b) Give the sign of f'' on each side of that point and name the intervals: convex where, concave where. (c) The inflection point, with both coordinates. (d) The stationary points, and the nature of each one — using f'', not a sketch. (e) One sentence a report would use for step 6.

title: Week 3 — Drills
text:
D4 (core). A second firm: R(q) = 30 ln(q + 1), C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25, both in € thousand, q ≥ 0. (a) Write π(q). (b) Write π'(q). (c) Solve π'(q) = 0. Leave it as an equation in q first, then solve the quadratic it becomes. (d) Confirm with π'' that it is a maximum. (e) Is the firm profitable at that quantity? Answer with a number.
D5 (core — the managerial reading). For the firm in D4, R'(q) is marginal revenue and C'(q) is marginal cost. (a) Write the condition π'(q) = 0 as R'(q) = C'(q), in words. (b) At q = 2 compute both. Which is larger, and what should the firm do?
D6 (stretch). A box with a square base and no lid must hold 32 m³. Minimise the material used. (Surface S = x² + 4xh, volume x²h = 32.)

title: Week 3 — Drills
text:
D7 (core — exam form). Evaluate, splitting term by term: (a) ∫ (q⁵ − 3q³ + 2)/q² dq (b) ∫ (4q³ − 6q + 5) dq (c) ∫ (2/q + 3√q) dq
D8 (core — exam form). Find f(q) given f'(q) = 12q² − 6q + 1 and f(2) = 20.
D8b (core — exam form, and the one that catches people). Find f(x) given f'(x) = 12x² − 4x and f(−3) = 17. Watch every sign.
D8c (core — the third rule). Evaluate, by asking first whether the top is the derivative of the bottom: (a) ∫ 1/(q − 4) dq (b) ∫ q/(q² + 5) dq (c) ∫ (2q + 3)/(q² + 3q − 1) dq (d) ∫ 5/(2q + 1) dq
D9 (core). Evaluate the definite integrals and say what each measures: (a) ∫₀²⁰ (0.8q + 3) dq where 0.8q + 3 is marginal cost. (b) ∫₁⁴ (6/q) dq. Leave the answer in terms of ln.
D9b (core — exam form). Evaluate ∫₀^(1/2) [ 1/(x − 1) + x/(x² − 1) ] dx, leaving the answer in terms of ln. Both terms are logs; neither is 1/x.
D10 (stretch). Marginal profit is π'(q) = 1200 − 8q. The firm currently makes 100 bikes. (a) By how much does profit change if output rises from 100 to 150? Compute it as a definite integral. (b) Check your answer against π(150) − π(100) using π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000.

title: Week 3 — Drills
text:
Added on 22 October, not covered in class: self-study for the midterm, with the addendum at the end of the week-3 slides.
D11 (core — the brief’s tariff question, different numbers). A firm has R(q) = 60 ln(q + 1) and C(q) = 0.25q² + 5q + 30, € thousand, q ≥ 0. Of the €5k that one more unit costs, €4k is a component imported from outside the EU. The EU imposes a 20% tariff on it. (a) Say which term of C the tariff moves, which it leaves alone, and why. Write the new cost C_t(q). (b) Find the profit-maximising output before and after the tariff. Confirm each is a maximum with π''. (c) Profit at each optimum, and the change in euro and in percent. (d) Check (c) in your head: tariff per unit × output. Why is the exact loss a little smaller? (e) One sentence for the Board.
D12 (core — a zero by bisection). For the firm of D11 with the tariff, π_t(q) = 60 ln(q + 1) − 0.25q² − 5.8q − 30. (a) Show that π_t changes sign between q = 0.75 and q = 0.8, and between q = 14 and q = 14.5. (b) Halve each interval until you can state both break-even outputs to one decimal place. (c) Before the tariff the break-evens were 0.76 and 15.57. What happened to the profitable window?
D13 (optional — the small-nation model). A small open economy: demand Q_d = 120 − 2p, domestic supply Q_s = 3p − 30 (Q in thousand units, p in €). The world price is €20. (a) Price and quantity with no trade (autarky). (b) Under free trade: quantity bought, made at home, imported. (c) A tariff of €5 a unit. The same three quantities. (d) Compute, as integrals or as areas: the loss of consumer surplus, the gain of domestic producers, the tariff revenue, and the two triangles — the protective and the consumption effect. Check that they add up. (e) What is the deadweight loss, and what does it mean in one sentence?
D14 (stretch — writing). In 150–200 words for a Board, explain why a tariff hurts a small open economy more than the triangles of D13 suggest. Find the channels yourself, and support each with a source you have actually read.



Solutions

D1. - Domain. A polynomial: all of ℝ. For a quantity, [0, +∞). - Zeros. −4q² + 1200q − 60,000 = 0; divide by −4: q² − 300q + 15,000 = 0. Δ = 90,000 − 60,000 = 30,000, √Δ ≈ 173.2. q = (300 ± 173.2)/2 → q ≈ 63.4 and q ≈ 236.6. - Sign. a = −4 < 0, so positive between the roots: π > 0 on (63.4, 236.6), negative outside. - Stationary point. π'(q) = −8q + 1200 = 0 → q = 150. - Nature. π''(q) = −8 < 0 for every q, so the stationary point is a maximum; the curve is concave everywhere. π(150) = −90,000 + 180,000 − 60,000 = **€30,000**. - Behaviour. lim (q→∞) π(q) = −∞: the −4q² term wins. There is no “sell more forever”. - Sketch. Downward parabola, crossing the axis at 63.4 and 236.6, peak (150, 30,000), intercept π(0) = −60,000. Label all four.
D2. (a) [0, +∞); C(0) = 25. That is fixed cost: what the firm pays having produced nothing. (b) AC(q) = 0.4q + 3 + 25/q, domain (0, +∞) — zero output has no average. lim (q→0⁺) AC = +∞ (fixed cost spread over almost nothing). lim (q→∞) AC = +∞ (the 0.4q term takes over). So AC falls, then rises: it has a minimum. (c) AC'(q) = 0.4 − 25/q² = 0 → q² = 62.5 → q ≈ 7.91. AC(7.91) = 3.16 + 3 + 3.16 = **9.32**; C'(7.91) = 0.8(7.91) + 3 = **9.32**. They are equal. Average cost is at its lowest exactly where marginal cost crosses it. Worth stating out loud: it is not a coincidence, it is what “average” means.
D2b. (a) ln(x + 3) needs x + 3 > 0, so the domain is (−3, +∞) — open, because ln 0 is undefined. (b) As x → −3⁺, ln(x+3) → −∞, and x² − 3x → 18, so f(x) → **−∞**. The line x = −3 is a vertical asymptote: the curve plunges down it. (c) As x → +∞ the x² term dominates everything, so f(x) → **+∞**. (d) f'(x) = 2x − 3 + 7/(x + 3) = (2x − 1)(x + 2)/(x + 3), zero at x = −2 and x = ½. So the curve comes up from −∞ along x = −3, reaches a local maximum at (−2, 10), dips to a local minimum at (½, ≈ 7.52), then rises to +∞. Two turns, not one. Draw the asymptote as a dashed vertical line: the marker looks for it.
D3. (a) f'(q) = 3q² − 24q + 36 = 3(q² − 8q + 12) = 3(q − 2)(q − 6) → q = 2, 6. f''(q) = 6q − 24: f''(2) = −12 < 0 → maximum, f(2) = 8 − 48 + 72 = 32. f''(6) = 12 > 0 → minimum, f(6) = 216 − 432 + 216 = 0. (b) f'' = 0 at q = 4, f(4) = 64 − 192 + 144 = 16; the curvature changes sign there, so it is an inflection. (c) Rises to (2, 32), falls to (6, 0), rises again; at q = 10, f = 1000 − 1200 + 360 = 160.
D3b. (a) f'(q) = 3q² − 12q + 9, f''(q) = 6q − 12. f'' = 0 at q = 2. (b) f''(1) = −6 < 0: concave on [0, 2). f''(3) = 6 > 0: convex on (2, ∞). The sign changes, so q = 2 is a genuine inflection and not just a zero. (c) f(2) = 8 − 24 + 18 + 4 = 6: inflection at (2, 6). Both coordinates, or the point is not located. (d) f'(q) = 3(q − 1)(q − 3) = 0 → q = 1, 3. f''(1) = −6 < 0 → maximum, f(1) = 8. f''(3) = 6 > 0 → minimum, f(3) = 4. Max at 1, inflection at 2, min at 3: the inflection sits between the turning points, where the fall is steepest. (e) “The curve is concave up to q = 2 and convex beyond it, with an inflection at (2, 6): the decline that begins at the maximum is steepest there, and slows afterwards until the minimum at q = 3.”
D4. (a) π(q) = 30 ln(q + 1) − 0.4q² − 3q − 25. (b) π'(q) = 30/(q + 1) − 0.8q − 3. (c) 30/(q + 1) = 0.8q + 3. Multiply by (q + 1): 30 = (0.8q + 3)(q + 1) = 0.8q² + 3.8q + 3 → 0.8q² + 3.8q − 27 = 0. Multiply by 5: 4q² + 19q − 135 = 0. Δ = 361 + 2160 = 2521, √Δ ≈ 50.21. q = (−19 ± 50.21)/8 → q ≈ 3.90 (the negative root is discarded: a quantity). (d) π''(q) = −30/(q + 1)² − 0.8 < 0 everywhere → maximum. (e) π(3.90) = 30 ln(4.90) − 0.4(15.21) − 3(3.90) − 25 = 47.68 − 6.08 − 11.70 − 25 = **€4.89k**. Profitable, but only just — the window is narrow, which is the point.
D5. (a) π' = R' − C' = 0 means R'(q) = C'(q): produce up to the point where the revenue from one more unit equals what that unit costs. (b) R'(2) = 30/3 = **10**; C'(2) = 0.8(2) + 3 = **4.6**. Marginal revenue is larger, so each extra unit still adds 10 − 4.6 = 5.4 — produce more, up to q ≈ 3.90.
D6. h = 32/x², so S = x² + 4x(32/x²) = x² + 128/x. S' = 2x − 128/x² = 0 → x³ = 64 → x = 4, h = 2. S'' = 2 + 256/x³ > 0 → minimum. S = 16 + 32 = **48 m²**.
D7. (a) Split first: (q⁵ − 3q³ + 2)/q² = q³ − 3q + 2q⁻². ∫ = q⁴/4 − 3q²/2 − 2/q + c. (b) q⁴ − 3q² + 5q + c. (c) ∫ 2/q dq = 2 ln|q|; ∫ 3q^{1/2} dq = 3 · (2/3) q^{3/2} = 2q^{3/2}. Total: 2 ln|q| + 2q^{3/2} + c. The exam’s integral is always this shape: divide term by term first, then each term is a power or a log.
D8. f(q) = 4q³ − 3q² + q + c. f(2) = 32 − 12 + 2 + c = 20 → c = −2. f(q) = 4q³ − 3q² + q − 2.
D8b. f(x) = 4x³ − 2x² + c. Now substitute carefully: f(−3) = 4(−27) − 2(9) + c = −108 − 18 + c = −126 + c = 17 → c = 143. f(x) = 4x³ − 2x² + 143. The trap is (−3)³ = −27 and (−3)² = +9. Two signs, two marks.
D8c. Ask each time: is the top the derivative of the bottom? (a) bottom differentiates to 1 → ln|q − 4| + c. (b) bottom differentiates to 2q, top is q, so a factor ½ is missing → ½ ln(q² + 5) + c. (No modulus needed: q² + 5 > 0 always.) (c) bottom differentiates to 2q + 3, which is exactly the top → ln|q² + 3q − 1| + c. (d) bottom differentiates to 2, top is 5, so 5/2 comes out → (5/2) ln|2q + 1| + c.
D9. (a) [0.4q² + 3q]₀²⁰ = 160 + 60 = **220**. Total variable cost of the first 20 bikes: adding up marginal cost gives total cost. (b) [6 ln q]₁⁴ = 6 ln 4 − 6 ln 1 = **6 ln 4 ≈ 8.32**.
D9b. Each term is a log. ∫ 1/(x−1) dx = ln|x−1|; ∫ x/(x²−1) dx = ½ ln|x²−1|. So the antiderivative is ln|x−1| + ½ ln|x²−1|, and
at ½ :  ln(½) + ½ ln(¾) = −0.6931 + ½(−0.2877) = −0.8370 at 0 :  ln 1 + ½ ln 1 = 0
= −0.8370, or exactly ln(½) + ½ ln(¾). Note the modulus: between 0 and ½ both x − 1 and x² − 1 are negative, and without the absolute value the logs are undefined. The exam’s model answer expects it.
D10. (a) ∫₁₀₀¹⁵⁰ (1200 − 8q) dq = [1200q − 4q²]₁₀₀¹⁵⁰ = (180,000 − 90,000) − (120,000 − 40,000) = 90,000 − 80,000 = **€10,000**. (b) π(150) = 30,000; π(100) = −40,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 = 20,000. Difference = **€10,000**. ✔ The integral of the marginal is the change in the total. That sentence is the whole of integration.
D11. (a) The tariff raises what the firm pays per unit for the component: 4 × 0.20 = €0.8k more per unit. That is the linear term, 5q → 5.8q. The quadratic term 0.25q² is the plant’s internal cost of running harder (overtime, congestion), not a purchase: untouched. The fixed cost 30 does not depend on output: untouched. C_t(q) = 0.25q² + 5.8q + 30. Revenue unchanged, assuming the firm cannot raise its price. (b) Before: π'(q) = 60/(q + 1) − 0.5q − 5 = 0 → 60 = (0.5q + 5)(q + 1) = 0.5q² + 5.5q + 5 → q² + 11q − 110 = 0. Δ = 121 + 440 = 561, √Δ ≈ 23.685, q* = (−11 + 23.685)/2 ≈ 6.34 (the negative root is outside the domain). After: 60 = (0.5q + 5.8)(q + 1) = 0.5q² + 6.3q + 5.8 → q² + 12.6q − 108.4 = 0. Δ = 158.76 + 433.6 = 592.36, √Δ ≈ 24.339, q_t* = (−12.6 + 24.339)/2 ≈ 5.87. Both: π''(q) = −60/(q + 1)² − 0.5 < 0 for every q ≥ 0, so each is a maximum (≈ −1.61 and −1.77). (c) π(6.34) = 60 ln 7.34 − 0.25(6.34)² − 5(6.34) − 30 ≈ **47.85**; π_t(5.87) ≈ **42.97**. Change −€4.88k, −10.2%. (d) 0.8 × 6.34 ≈ 5.07. The exact loss is smaller because the firm cuts output by half a unit and stops paying the tariff on what it no longer makes. (e) “The tariff costs us about €4.9k a month, a tenth of our profit; we should produce about 5.9 units instead of 6.3.”
D12. (a) π_t(0.75) ≈ −0.91, π_t(0.8) ≈ +0.47; π_t(14) ≈ +2.28, π_t(14.5) ≈ −2.21. Each pair has opposite signs, so π_t crosses zero inside each interval (it is continuous there). (b) Lower: π_t(0.775) ≈ −0.22 → between 0.775 and 0.8; π_t(0.7875) ≈ +0.13 → between 0.775 and 0.7875. Every number in there rounds to q ≈ 0.8 (exact 0.783). Upper: π_t(14.25) ≈ +0.06 → between 14.25 and 14.5; π_t(14.3) ≈ −0.39 → between 14.25 and 14.3: q ≈ 14.3 (exact 14.257). (c) From [0.76, 15.57] to [0.78, 14.26]: the window shrinks, mostly at the top. At high output the tariff is paid on many units, so the firm stops covering its costs much sooner.
D13. (a) 120 − 2p = 3p − 30 → p = 30, Q = 60. (b) At p = 20: bought Q_d = 80, made at home Q_s = 30, imported 50. (c) At p = 25: bought 70, made at home 45, imported 25. (d) ΔCS = ∫₂₀²⁵ (120 − 2p) dp = [120p − p²]₂₀²⁵ = 2375 − 2000 = **375**. ΔPS = ∫₂₀²⁵ (3p − 30) dp = [1.5p² − 30p]₂₀²⁵ = 187.5 − 0 = **187.5**. Revenue = 5 × 25 = **125**. Protective effect = ½ × 5 × (45 − 30) = **37.5**; consumption effect = ½ × 5 × (80 − 70) = **25**. Check: 187.5 + 125 + 37.5 + 25 = 375 ✔ (all in € thousand). (e) Deadweight loss = 37.5 + 25 = **62.5**: the part of the consumers’ loss that nobody gains — production done at home at more than the world price, and purchases that no longer happen.
D14. No model answer, on purpose: finding and judging the sources is the exercise. Check your paragraph against the method: each channel named precisely, a recent and reliable source cited Harvard, the way it reaches a firm’s costs or revenue, the direction, and what a Board should do. At least one channel should come back to the cost function of D11. Wikipedia is not a source.

title: Week 1 — Drills
text:
Exam format. Show all work. Core items are for everyone; stretch items for whoever finishes early. Solutions at the end, worked the way an examiner wants to see them.


D1 (core). Arno Bikes has fixed monthly costs of €60,000 and a variable cost of €400 per bike. Bikes sell at €1,000. (a) Write the cost function C(q) and the revenue function R(q). (b) Find the break-even quantity. (c) The landlord raises the rent so that fixed costs become €72,000. Find the new break-even quantity and state in one sentence what happened to the cost line in the (q, €) plane.
D2 (core). In the Tuscan e-bike market, demand is Q_d = 1200 − 2p and supply is Q_s = −300 + 3p (p in €, Q in bikes per month). (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) The region introduces a tax of €50 per bike paid by sellers, so that sellers now respond to the price they keep, p − 50. Write the new supply function and find the new equilibrium. (c) How much of the €50 tax is paid by buyers, in the form of a higher price?
D3 (stretch). A workshop assembles two models. Model A takes 2 hours, model B takes 3 hours; 1,200 hours are available per month and the plan is 500 bikes in total. Set up and solve the system giving the number of each model.



D3b (core — the syllabus asks for these and they are quick). Solve, and write each answer as an interval: (a) 3q − 12 > 0 (b) 5 − 2q ≥ 1 (c) 400q + 60,000 ≤ 1,000q (d) What does (c) say about Arno Bikes, in one clause?
D4 (core). A firm’s profit function is π(q) = −2q² + 600q − 40,000. (a) Find the quantities at which profit is zero. (b) For which quantities is the firm profitable? (c) Find the vertex of the parabola and interpret it.
D5 (core). Solve the inequalities: (a) x² − 7x + 10 ≤ 0 (b) 2x² + 3x − 2 > 0
D6 (stretch — the final-exam pattern). Factor numerator and denominator, then simplify: (x − 1)² / (x − x²). Evaluate the simplified expression at x = 1.1 and at x = 0.9 and comment on the sign.



D7 (core). (a) Simplify: ln(e³), log₂ 32, ln(a²b / c). (b) Solve for x: 3ˣ = 81; 10ˣ = 500 (three decimals).
D8 (core). Arno Bikes’ revenue is €1.2M and grows at 12% a year. (a) Write revenue after t years. (b) How many years to double? (c) How many years to reach €3M?
D9 (stretch). (a) Solve 5e^{0.03t} = 8 for t. (b) A competitor doubled revenue in 5 years. What constant annual growth rate does that imply?



D10 (core). (a) Battery cells must be 500 Wh ± 15 Wh. Write the condition with an absolute value and as an interval. Is a 483 Wh cell acceptable? (b) Solve |x − 3| > 2.
D11 (core — notation for the exam). Write as intervals: (a) x ≥ −3; (b) x > −3; (c) −3 < x ≤ 5. Then state the domain, as an interval, of (d) f(x) = √(x + 3) and (e) g(x) = ln(x − 1).



Solutions

D1. (a) C(q) = 60,000 + 400q; R(q) = 1,000q. (b) R = C → 1,000q = 60,000 + 400q → 600q = 60,000 → q = 100 bikes. (Contribution per bike €600; 60,000 / 600 = 100.) (c) 1,000q = 72,000 + 400q → q = 120. The cost line shifted up in parallel by €12,000 (same slope, higher intercept); the crossing with the revenue line moved right.
D2. (a) 1200 − 2p = −300 + 3p → 1500 = 5p → p = €300; Q = 1200 − 600 = 600. (b) Q_s = −300 + 3(p − 50) = −450 + 3p. Then 1200 − 2p = −450 + 3p → 1650 = 5p → p = €330, Q = 540. (c) Buyers pay €330 instead of €300: €30 of the €50 is passed to buyers; sellers keep 330 − 50 = 280, i.e. bear €20.
D3. Let x = model A, y = model B. 2x + 3y = 1200, x + y = 500. From the second, x = 500 − y; substitute: 1000 − 2y + 3y = 1200 → y = 200, x = 300. 300 of A, 200 of B.
D3b. (a) 3q > 12 → q > 4 → (4, +∞). (b) −2q ≥ −4; dividing by a negative flips the sign → q ≤ 2 → (−∞, 2], or [0, 2] for a quantity. (c) 60,000 ≤ 600q → q ≥ 100 → [100, +∞). (d) It is the break-even condition written as an inequality: at 100 bikes or more the firm is not losing money. The one that costs marks is (b): multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses it.
D4. (a) Divide by −2: q² − 300q + 20,000 = 0. Discriminant 300² − 4·20,000 = 90,000 − 80,000 = 10,000, √ = 100. q = (300 ± 100)/2 → q = 100 and q = 200. (b) Downward parabola (a = −2 < 0) is positive between its roots: 100 < q < 200. (c) Vertex at q = −b/(2a) = −600/(−4) = 150; π(150) = −2·22,500 + 90,000 − 40,000 = **€5,000**. Maximum profit is €5,000 at 150 units; the window is narrow, the business is fragile.
D5. (a) Roots of x² − 7x + 10: (x − 2)(x − 5) → 2 and 5. Upward parabola ≤ 0 between roots: 2 ≤ x ≤ 5, i.e. [2, 5]. (b) Roots: x = (−3 ± √(9 + 16))/4 = (−3 ± 5)/4 → x = 1/2 and x = −2. Upward parabola > 0 outside the roots: x < −2 or x > 1/2.
D6. x − x² = x(1 − x) = −x(x − 1). So (x − 1)² / (−x(x − 1)) = −(x − 1)/x for x ≠ 0, 1. At x = 1.1: −0.1/1.1 ≈ −0.091. At x = 0.9: −(−0.1)/0.9 ≈ +0.111. The expression changes sign across x = 1 — approaching 1 from the right it is a small negative number, from the left a small positive number. (This is the algebra behind the one-sided limits the final exam asks for: factor, cancel, then look at the sign of what is left. The limit from the right is 0⁻.)
D7. (a) ln(e³) = 3; log₂ 32 = 5 (2⁵ = 32); ln(a²b/c) = 2 ln a + ln b − ln c. (b) 3ˣ = 81 = 3⁴ → x = 4. 10ˣ = 500 → x = log₁₀ 500 = **2.699**.
D8. (a) R(t) = 1.2 · 1.12ᵗ (€M). (b) 1.12ᵗ = 2 → t ln 1.12 = ln 2 → t = 0.6931 / 0.1133 = **6.1 years**. (c) 1.12ᵗ = 2.5 → t = ln 2.5 / ln 1.12 = 0.9163 / 0.1133 = **8.1 years**.
D9. (a) e^{0.03t} = 1.6 → 0.03t = ln 1.6 = 0.4700 → t ≈ 15.7. (b) (1 + g)⁵ = 2 → 1 + g = 2^{1/5} = e^{(ln 2)/5} = e^{0.1386} = 1.1487 → g ≈ 14.9% a year.
D10. (a) |c − 500| ≤ 15 ↔︎ 485 ≤ c ≤ 515, i.e. [485, 515]. 483 < 485: not acceptable. (b) |x − 3| > 2 ↔︎ x − 3 > 2 or x − 3 < −2 ↔︎ x > 5 or x < 1.
D11. (a) [−3, +∞); (b) (−3, +∞); (c) (−3, 5]. (d) Need x + 3 ≥ 0 → [−3, +∞). (e) Need x − 1 > 0 → (1, +∞). (Square bracket when the endpoint is included, round when it is not or when it is ±∞. The resit asks exactly this.)

title: Week 1 — Drills
text:
D1 (core). Arno Bikes has fixed monthly costs of €60,000 and a variable cost of €400 per bike. Bikes sell at €1,000. (a) Write the cost function C(q) and the revenue function R(q). (b) Find the break-even quantity. (c) The landlord raises the rent so that fixed costs become €72,000. Find the new break-even quantity and state in one sentence what happened to the cost line in the (q, €) plane.
D2 (core). In the Tuscan e-bike market, demand is Q_d = 1200 − 2p and supply is Q_s = −300 + 3p (p in €, Q in bikes per month). (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) The region introduces a tax of €50 per bike paid by sellers, so that sellers now respond to the price they keep, p − 50. Write the new supply function and find the new equilibrium. (c) How much of the €50 tax is paid by buyers, in the form of a higher price?

text:

title: Week 1 — Drills
text:
D7 (core). (a) Simplify: ln(e³), log₂ 32, ln(a²b / c). (b) Solve for x: 3ˣ = 81; 10ˣ = 500 (three decimals).
D8 (core). Arno Bikes’ revenue is €1.2M and grows at 12% a year. (a) Write revenue after t years. (b) How many years to double? (c) How many years to reach €3M?
D9 (stretch). (a) Solve 5e^{0.03t} = 8 for t. (b) A competitor doubled revenue in 5 years. What constant annual growth rate does that imply?

title: Week 1 — Drills
text:
D10 (core). (a) Battery cells must be 500 Wh ± 15 Wh. Write the condition with an absolute value and as an interval. Is a 483 Wh cell acceptable? (b) Solve |x − 3| > 2.
D11 (core — notation for the exam). Write as intervals: (a) x ≥ −3; (b) x > −3; (c) −3 < x ≤ 5. Then state the domain, as an interval, of (d) f(x) = √(x + 3) and (e) g(x) = ln(x − 1).



Solutions

D1. (a) C(q) = 60,000 + 400q; R(q) = 1,000q. (b) R = C → 1,000q = 60,000 + 400q → 600q = 60,000 → q = 100 bikes. (Contribution per bike €600; 60,000 / 600 = 100.) (c) 1,000q = 72,000 + 400q → q = 120. The cost line shifted up in parallel by €12,000 (same slope, higher intercept); the crossing with the revenue line moved right.
D2. (a) 1200 − 2p = −300 + 3p → 1500 = 5p → p = €300; Q = 1200 − 600 = 600. (b) Q_s = −300 + 3(p − 50) = −450 + 3p. Then 1200 − 2p = −450 + 3p → 1650 = 5p → p = €330, Q = 540. (c) Buyers pay €330 instead of €300: €30 of the €50 is passed to buyers; sellers keep 330 − 50 = 280, i.e. bear €20.
D3. Let x = model A, y = model B. 2x + 3y = 1200, x + y = 500. From the second, x = 500 − y; substitute: 1000 − 2y + 3y = 1200 → y = 200, x = 300. 300 of A, 200 of B.
D3b. (a) 3q > 12 → q > 4 → (4, +∞). (b) −2q ≥ −4; dividing by a negative flips the sign → q ≤ 2 → (−∞, 2], or [0, 2] for a quantity. (c) 60,000 ≤ 600q → q ≥ 100 → [100, +∞). (d) It is the break-even condition written as an inequality: at 100 bikes or more the firm is not losing money. The one that costs marks is (b): multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses it.
D4. (a) Divide by −2: q² − 300q + 20,000 = 0. Discriminant 300² − 4·20,000 = 90,000 − 80,000 = 10,000, √ = 100. q = (300 ± 100)/2 → q = 100 and q = 200. (b) Downward parabola (a = −2 < 0) is positive between its roots: 100 < q < 200. (c) Vertex at q = −b/(2a) = −600/(−4) = 150; π(150) = −2·22,500 + 90,000 − 40,000 = **€5,000**. Maximum profit is €5,000 at 150 units; the window is narrow, the business is fragile.
D5. (a) Roots of x² − 7x + 10: (x − 2)(x − 5) → 2 and 5. Upward parabola ≤ 0 between roots: 2 ≤ x ≤ 5, i.e. [2, 5]. (b) Roots: x = (−3 ± √(9 + 16))/4 = (−3 ± 5)/4 → x = 1/2 and x = −2. Upward parabola > 0 outside the roots: x < −2 or x > 1/2.
D6. x − x² = x(1 − x) = −x(x − 1). So (x − 1)² / (−x(x − 1)) = −(x − 1)/x for x ≠ 0, 1. At x = 1.1: −0.1/1.1 ≈ −0.091. At x = 0.9: −(−0.1)/0.9 ≈ +0.111. The expression changes sign across x = 1 — approaching 1 from the right it is a small negative number, from the left a small positive number. (This is the algebra behind the one-sided limits the final exam asks for: factor, cancel, then look at the sign of what is left. The limit from the right is 0⁻.)
D7. (a) ln(e³) = 3; log₂ 32 = 5 (2⁵ = 32); ln(a²b/c) = 2 ln a + ln b − ln c. (b) 3ˣ = 81 = 3⁴ → x = 4. 10ˣ = 500 → x = log₁₀ 500 = **2.699**.
D8. (a) R(t) = 1.2 · 1.12ᵗ (€M). (b) 1.12ᵗ = 2 → t ln 1.12 = ln 2 → t = 0.6931 / 0.1133 = **6.1 years**. (c) 1.12ᵗ = 2.5 → t = ln 2.5 / ln 1.12 = 0.9163 / 0.1133 = **8.1 years**.
D9. (a) e^{0.03t} = 1.6 → 0.03t = ln 1.6 = 0.4700 → t ≈ 15.7. (b) (1 + g)⁵ = 2 → 1 + g = 2^{1/5} = e^{(ln 2)/5} = e^{0.1386} = 1.1487 → g ≈ 14.9% a year.
D10. (a) |c − 500| ≤ 15 ↔︎ 485 ≤ c ≤ 515, i.e. [485, 515]. 483 < 485: not acceptable. (b) |x − 3| > 2 ↔︎ x − 3 > 2 or x − 3 < −2 ↔︎ x > 5 or x < 1.
D11. (a) [−3, +∞); (b) (−3, +∞); (c) (−3, 5]. (d) Need x + 3 ≥ 0 → [−3, +∞). (e) Need x − 1 > 0 → (1, +∞). (Square bracket when the endpoint is included, round when it is not or when it is ±∞. The resit asks exactly this.)

title: Homework 5 — bring it to the next session
text:
No session of mine follows this one, so this homework is not corrected in class. Send a photo or a scan of your working by email by Wednesday 28 October, 23:59, and it comes back with written comments before the midterm deadline.
The last homework of my half. Lighter than usual on purpose: Reading Week is for the midterm, which is due Sunday 1 November on Turnitin.
Part 1 on paper, Part 2 typed. Expect about two hours.


H1 (pricing). A 6-year bond, 5% annual coupon, face €100. (a) Its price at a yield of 7%. (b) At 5%. (c) At 3%. (d) State in one line the rule connecting coupon, yield and price that your three answers illustrate.
H2 (zero-coupon). A zero pays €100 in 12 years, yield 4%. (a) Its price. (b) The price if the yield rises to 5%, and the percentage change. (c) Why is that percentage change larger than for a coupon bond of the same maturity?
H3 (duration). For the 6-year 5% bond at a 7% yield (H1a): (a) Macaulay duration, with the table of weights. (b) Modified duration. (c) The estimated price change for a 75 basis point rise in yield.
H4 (duration, the rules). Without computing, say what happens to duration when, other things equal: (a) maturity lengthens (b) the coupon rises (c) the yield rises One clause of justification each.
H5 (convexity). A bond has P = 100, D_mod = 6.50, C = 55.0. (a) Estimate the price after a 2% rise in yield, using duration only. (b) Now with the convexity term as well. (c) Which of the two estimates is closer to the truth, and in which direction was the first one wrong?
H6 (portfolio). A reserve holds €300,000 of a bond with D_mod = 8.1 and €700,000 of one with D_mod = 2.4. (a) The portfolio’s modified duration. (b) The estimated change in value if yields fall by 0.5%. (c) The Board wants the portfolio’s duration down to 3.0 without selling either bond entirely. Which way must the weights move? A sentence, no algebra required.
H7 (immunisation — beyond the syllabus). Arno Bikes must pay €2,000,000 in exactly 5 years. It can buy 3-year and 9-year zero-coupon bonds, both yielding 4%. (a) How much must it set aside today? (b) The share in each zero that makes the portfolio’s duration 5 years, the euros in each, and what each zero pays at maturity. (c) The day after the purchase, yields jump to 5%. The value of the portfolio at year 5 — the 3-year zero’s payment reinvested for two years, the 9-year zero with four years still to run — against the €2,000,000 owed. (d) In one sentence: why must the treasurer look at this portfolio again next year, even if rates never move?



Arno Bikes keeps €1M in the bond reserve described in H6. The Board has read that rates may rise by a point over the next year and has asked: should we be worried?
Answer with: the loss duration predicts, one sentence on why that figure is an estimate and not a fact, what convexity does to it, and what you would change about the portfolio if the Board’s view is right. End with what you would need to see to change your recommendation.




Every price shows the annuity part and the redemption part separately.
The duration table has a weights column that sums to 1. If it does not, something is wrong before the duration is.
Modified duration is distinguished from Macaulay duration everywhere, including in the units.
The convexity term is ½ C (Δy)² — the half and the square are both easy to drop and both change the answer.
In H7 the duration you match is Macaulay, in years, against the date of the payment — not the modified duration.

This is a rehearsal of the midterm. A firm has a cost function C(q) = 0.2q² + 4q + 80 and a revenue function R(q) = 40 ln(q + 1), both in € thousand per month.
Write a short report for the Board that:

States the profit function and studies it: domain, sign, the quantity that maximises it, and proof that it is a maximum.
Includes a sketch of the profit function, hand-drawn, with axes labelled and the maximum marked.
Answers this question in plain English: at the optimum, how much room for error does the firm have? Support it with the profit at the optimum and at one quantity either side.
Ends with a recommendation of one sentence.

Structure it with headings. Numbers in the text, working in an appendix. The midterm asks for a longer version of exactly this, with an added qualitative section and Harvard referencing — which we brief next.

π'' is computed and its sign is stated, not just the formula: that is what proves maximum or minimum.

Every integral is split term by term before integrating, and every indefinite integral ends in + c.

title: How to work
section: Homework
text:
Homework
Set every Thursday, corrected together in class the following Thursday. Two parts, 2–3 hours in total:

A drill set on paper. Bring the paper itself: nothing is handed in or emailed. Show all work: the marks in the exam are for the method, and so is the feedback here.

title: Homework 2 — bring it to the next session
text:
Bring it to class, done on paper. Nothing to hand in or send: the first 15–20 minutes of next session are spent going through it together at the board — you walk us through your working, we correct it there and then. Mistakes are the useful part, so bring what you tried even where you got stuck.
Two parts. Part 1 on paper. Part 2 a short typed text. Expect 2–3 hours. Formative: not graded, but the walkthrough is where you find out what you have really understood.


H1. State the domain of each, as an interval, and say in one clause what the restriction means for a firm. (a) f(q) = √(2q − 30) (b) g(q) = ln(40 − q) (c) h(q) = (q + 5)/(q² − 9)
H2. A workshop has C(q) = 0.4q² + 8q + 200 and sells at a fixed price of €60. (a) Write R(q) and π(q). (b) Evaluate π(30), π(65), π(100). (c) From those three numbers alone, between which two quantities must the best output lie? Say how you know, without computing it.
H3. Evaluate, showing the factoring step: (a) lim (q→4) (q² − 16)/(q − 4) (b) lim (q→2) (q² − q − 2)/(q − 2) (c) lim (q→0⁺) (q² + 3q)/q
H4 (exam form). Evaluate lim (q→2⁺) (q − 2)²/(2q − q²). Write out the factoring and comment on the sign of each factor as q approaches 2 from above.
H5. Evaluate and give the business reading of each: (a) lim (q→∞) (0.4q² + 8q + 200)/q — average cost per unit as the run gets long. Why does this one not settle down, and what does that say about the workshop? (b) lim (q→∞) (200 + 15q)/q.
H6. Differentiate: (a) π(q) = −3q² + 900q − 40,000 (b) C(q) = 0.4q² + 8q + 200 (c) R(q) = 45 ln(q + 1) (d) f(q) = 2q⁴ − 6q² + q − 9
H7. For π(q) = −3q² + 900q − 40,000: (a) Compute π'(50) and write the one sentence you would say to the owner. (b) Compute π'(200) and do the same. (c) Solve π'(q) = 0 and state what that quantity is.
H8 (exam form). Find f(q) given f'(q) = 9q² − 4q + 2 and f(1) = 10.



You are the plant manager of Arno Bikes. Last month you produced 80 bikes. The Board has asked for one number: should the next bike be built?
Answer it with the derivative. Give the marginal profit at 80, say what it means in euros, and state the quantity at which the answer changes from yes to no. Then add one sentence on what you would need to check before trusting the number — the model says demand is p = 1600 − 4q and cost is 60,000 + 400q; say which of those two you would verify first, and why.
Numbers and their meaning. No formulas in the text; put the working in an appendix if you want it seen.




Every domain is written as an interval, with [ or ( chosen deliberately.
Every limit that starts as 0/0 shows the factoring before the substitution.
Every derivative is done term by term, and the constant term has disappeared.
In H8 the constant of integration is found from the given condition, not left as c.
The memo says what one more unit does, in euros, and where the sign changes.





H1, H5 are the domain and asymptote questions the resit asks in exactly this form.
H3, H4 are the limit item of the final exam’s Q5: a 0/0 that factors, and a one-sided limit.
H6, H8 are the other two Q5 items: differentiate term by term, and recover a function from its derivative with an initial condition.
H2, H7 and the memo are the midterm: study a profit function and write the result for a Board.

title: Homework 4 — bring it to the next session
text:
Bring it to class, done on paper. Nothing to hand in or send: the first 15–20 minutes of next session are spent going through it together at the board — you walk us through your working, we correct it there and then. Mistakes are the useful part, so bring what you tried even where you got stuck.
Two parts. Part 1 on paper, with a calculator. Part 2 typed. Expect 2–3 hours.
Money to the cent, rates to two decimals in a percentage. Show the formula before the number every time: the exam gives marks for the method.


H1. €12,000 is invested for 5 years at 7%. (a) Final amount with simple interest. (b) With annual compounding. (c) The difference, and one line on where it comes from.
H2. €20,000 at 6% nominal for 3 years, compounded (a) annually (b) quarterly (c) monthly. Give the three final amounts.
H3 (EAR). Compute the effective annual rate of 9% nominal compounded (a) semi-annually (b) quarterly (c) monthly (d) continuously. Then say in one line why a borrower should always ask for the EAR.
H4 (resit form). Select the correct alternative and justify in one line. Two loans quote the same nominal rate. Loan A compounds monthly, loan B annually. For the borrower: (i) A is cheaper (ii) B is cheaper (iii) they cost the same
H5 (present value). (a) What is €25,000 receivable in 6 years worth today at 8%? (b) How much must be invested today at 5% to have €50,000 in 10 years?
H6 (annuity). A lease requires €9,000 at the end of each year for 7 years. Your cost of capital is 6%. (a) The present value of the lease. (b) The seller offers to sell the asset outright for €52,000. Which is cheaper in today’s money, and by how much?
H7 (perpetuity). A building is let for €36,000 a year, for ever, first payment in one year. (a) Its value at a 6% required return. (b) At 8%. (c) One line on why the two differ so much.
H8 (NPV — the decision). A project costs €900,000 now and returns €260,000, €300,000, €340,000 and €360,000 at the end of the next four years. The cost of capital is 10%. (a) Lay out a table: year, flow, discount factor, present value. (b) The NPV. (c) Accept or reject, in one sentence. (d) Recompute at 18%. What has changed, and what is the name of the rate between the two where the sign flips?
H9 (growing perpetuity — what a firm is worth). A small competitor expects a free cash flow of €240,000 next year, growing 2.5% a year for ever. Your required return is 10%. (a) Its value today. (b) Its value if growth is 3.5% instead. By how much, in euros, does one point of growth move the price? (c) One line: why does the formula give nonsense if someone assumes growth of 10% or more?
H10 (challenge — a function study, on money). For the project in H8, write NPV(r) as a function of the discount rate, r ≥ 0, and study it: NPV(0) and what it means; the limit as r → ∞ and the asymptote; why it is decreasing; where it changes sign (you have its value at 10% and at 18%); a sketch with those points. Finish with one sentence on what the sketch says about the project’s margin of safety.



The Board of Arno Bikes has been offered the assembly line from class: €2.4M now, returning €700k, €800k, €900k and €1,000k over four years. A Board member says: “It returns €3.4M on a €2.4M outlay. That is a million of profit — obviously we do it.”
Write the memo that corrects this, politely and with numbers. Say what is wrong with adding the flows up, give the NPV at the firm’s 9% cost of capital, and state the rate at which the answer would change. End with a recommendation and one condition you would attach to it.
No formulas in the text. Put the discounting table in an appendix if you want it seen.




Every compound-interest answer states m (how many times a year) explicitly.
Every EAR is computed from the nominal rate, never compared to it directly.
Every present value shows the discount factor separately from the flow.
The NPV table has a row for year 0, with a factor of 1.
The memo names the number that makes the Board member’s reasoning wrong, and does it in one clause.





H1–H4 are the resit’s multiple-choice-with-justification block, in the exact form.
H5–H7 are the present-value machinery every financial-maths question rests on.
H9 goes one step beyond the syllabus: the same perpetuity, with growth — how a whole firm is priced.
H10 is the week-3 function study applied to the NPV curve: the final and the resit each ask one of the two, and this is where they meet.
H8 and the memo are the NPV question, and the register the midterm asks for: a decision, defended with numbers, for people who will not read an appendix.

title: Revision set — weeks 1 to 4
text:
Everything so far, in exam form, in one place. Published after session 4 so that you have it for Reading Week; it sits next to Homework 4 but it is not homework and nothing is handed in. Solutions at the end, worked the way the examiner wants to see them.
What it is for. Two things are coming: the midterm paper, due Sunday 1 November (the study of a cost, a revenue and a profit function, written up for a Board), and the final exam’s calculus question, five items done by hand with a calculator and no notes. Every item below rehearses one of those two or the resit’s multiple-choice form. The tag after each number says which.
How to use it. On paper, with a calculator, timed: twelve minutes for a function study, four for an integral or a limit, six for an NPV table. Do a section, then open the solutions and mark yourself as an examiner would: method first, number second. Where you were wrong, redo the item from a blank page the next day. Watching the lesson recordings is useful for the ideas; the marks come from the items you can do without them. Expect five to six hours in total; two sittings is sensible.
Numbers. Money to the cent, rates to two decimals in a percentage, everything else to three decimals unless it is exact.


R1 (midterm Q2–Q3 — the shapes you will study). A bike workshop has fixed costs of €45,000 a month and a variable cost of €250 per bike. It sells at €550. (a) Write C(q) and R(q) and find the break-even quantity. (b) The market has demand Q_d = 1500 − 5p and supply Q_s = −300 + 4p. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
R2 (midterm Q3 — sign of a profit function). π(q) = −3q² + 420q − 12,000. (a) The quantities at which profit is zero. (b) The interval on which the firm is profitable. (c) The vertex, and what it means.
R3 (week-4 arithmetic rests on this). Solve for t, three decimals: (a) 15,000 × 1.08ᵗ = 30,000 (b) e^{0.05t} = 2.5 (c) Simplify ln(a³ / √b).
R4 (final Q5 uses the notation). (a) Solve |x − 8| ≤ 3 and write it as an interval. (b) Solve |3x + 2| > 7 and write it as a union of intervals.



R5 (midterm Q2 — domain, step 1 of the study). Give the domain of each as an interval, and say in one clause what the restriction means for a firm: (a) f(q) = √(2q − 6) (b) g(q) = ln(10 − q) (c) h(q) = (q + 1)/(q² − 4)
R6 (final Q5 — the one-sided limit, exact form). Evaluate lim (q→4⁺) (q − 4)² / (4q − q²). Factor, simplify, then say the sign the expression has just above 4.
R7 (final Q5 — limits at −∞). Evaluate: (a) lim (q→−∞) (2q² − 5q + 1)/(4q² + 3) (b) lim (q→−∞) (5q + 2)/(q² − 3) (c) lim (q→−∞) (q³ + 2)/(q² − 1)



R8 (midterm Q2–Q3 — the derivatives you will need). Differentiate: (a) 4q³ − 6q² + 1/q (b) ln(3q² + 1) (c) (3q + 1)⁴
R9 (final Q5 — the indefinite integral, exact form). Evaluate ∫ (3q⁴ − 4q + 6)/q² dq. Split term by term before integrating.
R10 (final Q5 — recover f from f′, exact form). Find f(q) given f′(q) = 8q³ − 6q + 2 and f(2) = 30.
R11 (final Q5 — the definite integral with logs, exact form). Evaluate ∫₂⁴ [2/q + 1/(q − 1)] dq, leaving the answer in terms of ln, then as a number.



R12 (midterm Q3 — the full study). Study π(q) = −5q² + 900q − 28,000 completely and sketch it. In this order: domain · zeros · sign · π′ and the stationary point · π″ and its nature · behaviour as q → ∞ · a labelled sketch.
R13 (midterm Q2–Q3 — the case’s own shape, with other numbers). C(q) = 0.25q² + 3q + 35 and R(q) = 33 ln(q + 1), both in € thousand a month, q ≥ 0. (a) Write π(q) and π′(q). (b) Solve π′(q) = 0, showing the quadratic it reduces to. (c) Confirm the nature of the point with π″. (d) Show that marginal revenue equals marginal cost there, and say in one line why that had to happen. (e) Profit at the optimum and at one unit either side. One sentence for the Board on the room for error.
R14 (midterm Q2 — convexity and inflection, the step people skip). f(q) = q³ − 15q² + 63q, q ≥ 0. (a) Stationary points and their nature, from the sign of f′. (b) Where f″ changes sign, and the point of inflection. (c) Sketch, marking all three points and the intervals where the curve is concave and convex.



R15 (resit — simple vs compound). €9,000 for 6 years at 5%: (a) simple interest; (b) compounded annually; (c) compounded quarterly. One line on why (c) > (b) > (a).
R16 (resit — select and justify). A depositor is offered 7% nominal compounded quarterly, or 7.1% compounded annually. Which is better for the depositor? (i) the first (ii) the second (iii) they are equivalent. Justify in one line with the number that decides it.
R17 (resit — present value). (a) What is €30,000 receivable in 4 years worth today at 6%? (b) An annuity pays €4,000 at the end of each year for 5 years; at 6%, what is it worth today? (c) The same €4,000, for ever. What is it worth, and why is the gap to (b) so large?
R18 (the NPV decision). A project costs €500,000 now and returns €150,000, €180,000, €200,000 and €120,000 at the end of the next four years. The cost of capital is 8%. (a) Lay out the table: year, flow, discount factor, present value. Row for year 0. (b) The NPV, and accept or reject in one sentence. (c) Recompute at 14%. The sign has changed: what is the name of the rate in between where it flips, and roughly where is it?
R19 (where the rate comes from). A firm is financed half by equity and half by debt. Shareholders expect 11%, the bank charges 5%, the tax rate is 30%. (a) The weighted average cost of capital. (b) One line: why does the tax rate appear on the debt side only?



R20. Two loans quote the same nominal rate; A compounds monthly, B annually. For the borrower: (i) A is cheaper (ii) B is cheaper (iii) they cost the same.
R21. The discount rate rises from 5% to 8%. The present value of €1,000 due in ten years: (i) rises (ii) falls (iii) is unchanged, since the €1,000 has not changed.
R22. A perpetuity pays €6,000 a year. If the required return doubles, its value: (i) doubles (ii) halves (iii) falls, but by less than half.
R23. At q = 12, f′(12) = 0 and f″(12) = −4. The point is: (i) a maximum (ii) a minimum (iii) an inflection point.



Solutions

R1. (a) C(q) = 45,000 + 250q, R(q) = 550q. Break-even: 550q = 45,000 + 250q → 300q = 45,000 → q = 150 bikes. (b) 1500 − 5p = −300 + 4p → 9p = 1800 → p = €200, Q = 1500 − 1000 = **500 bikes**.
R2. (a) −3q² + 420q − 12,000 = 0 → divide by −3: q² − 140q + 4,000 = 0 → q = (140 ± √(19,600 − 16,000))/2 = (140 ± 60)/2 → q = 40 and q = 100. (b) Parabola opens downward (coefficient −3), so profit is positive between the zeros: 40 < q < 100. (c) Vertex at q = −b/2a = 420/6 = 70; π(70) = −14,700 + 29,400 − 12,000 = **2,700**. The most the firm can make, and the quantity at which it makes it.
R3. (a) 1.08ᵗ = 2 → t = ln 2 / ln 1.08 = 0.693147/0.076961 = **9.006** years. (b) 0.05t = ln 2.5 = 0.916291 → t = **18.326**. (c) ln(a³) − ln(b^{1/2}) = **3 ln a − ½ ln b**.
R4. (a) −3 ≤ x − 8 ≤ 3 → [5, 11]. (b) 3x + 2 > 7 → x > 5/3; or 3x + 2 < −7 → x < −3. (−∞, −3) ∪ (5/3, ∞).
R5. (a) 2q − 6 ≥ 0 → [3, ∞): the function is not defined below 3 units. (b) 10 − q > 0 → (−∞, 10): beyond 10 the log has nothing to take; a capacity ceiling. (c) q² − 4 ≠ 0 → q ≠ ±2, i.e. (−∞, −2) ∪ (−2, 2) ∪ (2, ∞): the function blows up at 2 (vertical asymptote); negative q is outside the business reading anyway.
R6. 4q − q² = q(4 − q) = −q(q − 4). So (q − 4)²/(−q(q − 4)) = −(q − 4)/q = (4 − q)/q for q ≠ 0, 4. As q → 4⁺, the numerator 4 − q → 0 from below (negative) and the denominator → 4: the expression is negative and tends to 0. The limit is 0, approached from the negative side.
R7. Divide by the highest power of q in the denominator. (a) (2 − 5/q + 1/q²)/(4 + 3/q²) → **1/2**. (b) (5/q + 2/q²)/(1 − 3/q²) → 0/1 = **0**. (c) (q + 2/q²)/(1 − 1/q²): numerator → −∞, denominator → 1: −∞.
R8. (a) 12q² − 12q − 1/q² (write 1/q = q⁻¹ first). (b) Outside is ln(·), inside is 3q² + 1: (1/(3q² + 1)) × 6q = **6q/(3q² + 1)**. (c) 4(3q + 1)³ × 3 = **12(3q + 1)³**.
R9. Split: 3q⁴/q² − 4q/q² + 6/q² = 3q² − 4/q + 6q⁻². Integrate term by term: q³ − 4 ln|q| + 6q⁻¹/(−1) + c = **q³ − 4 ln|q| − 6/q + c**.
R10. f(q) = 2q⁴ − 3q² + 2q + c. f(2) = 32 − 12 + 4 + c = 24 + c = 30 → c = 6. f(q) = 2q⁴ − 3q² + 2q + 6.
R11. ∫ 2/q dq = 2 ln q, ∫ 1/(q − 1) dq = ln(q − 1) (the top is the derivative of the bottom). So [2 ln q + ln(q − 1)]₂⁴ = (2 ln 4 + ln 3) − (2 ln 2 + ln 1) = 2 ln 4 − 2 ln 2 + ln 3 = 2 ln 2 + ln 3 = **ln 12 ≈ 2.485**.
R12. 1. Domain: q ≥ 0 (all reals for the function; the business reading starts at 0). 2. Zeros: q² − 180q + 5,600 = 0 → q = (180 ± √(32,400 − 22,400))/2 = (180 ± 100)/2 → 40 and 140. Vertical intercept π(0) = −28,000 (the fixed cost). 3. Sign: negative on [0, 40), positive on (40, 140), negative beyond 140. 4. π′(q) = −10q + 900 = 0 → q = 90; π(90) = −40,500 + 81,000 − 28,000 = **12,500**. 5. π″(q) = −10 < 0 everywhere: concave, so q = 90 is a maximum (and the only one). 6. No inflection (the second derivative never changes sign). As q → ∞, π → −∞: the −5q² term wins. 7. Sketch: downward parabola through (0, −28,000), (40, 0), (140, 0), peak at (90, 12,500), symmetric about q = 90.
R13. (a) π(q) = 33 ln(q + 1) − 0.25q² − 3q − 35; π′(q) = 33/(q + 1) − 0.5q − 3. (b) 33/(q + 1) = 0.5q + 3 → 33 = (0.5q + 3)(q + 1) = 0.5q² + 3.5q + 3 → 0.5q² + 3.5q − 30 = 0 → q² + 7q − 60 = 0 → (q + 12)(q − 5) = 0 → q = 5 (the negative root is outside the domain). (c) π″(q) = −33/(q + 1)² − 0.5 < 0 for every q: concave everywhere, so q = 5 is the maximum. Numerically π″(5) = −33/36 − 0.5 = −1.417. (d) R′(5) = 33/6 = 5.5; C′(5) = 0.5 × 5 + 3 = 5.5. Equal, because π′ = R′ − C′ and we set π′ = 0: the optimum is exactly where one more unit adds as much to revenue as to cost. (e) π(5) = 33 ln 6 − 6.25 − 15 − 35 = 59.128 − 56.25 = **€2,878** (2.878 thousand); π(4) = 33 ln 5 − 51 = 53.112 − 51 = €2,111; π(6) = 33 ln 7 − 62 = 64.215 − 62 = €2,215. The peak is flat: a unit either way costs €700–800 of a €2,900 profit. For the Board: the optimum is five units a month, but it is a thin optimum — the firm is barely profitable at the best quantity, and the fixed cost, not the quantity, is the number to work on.
R14. (a) f′(q) = 3q² − 30q + 63 = 3(q² − 10q + 21) = 3(q − 3)(q − 7). Positive below 3, negative between 3 and 7, positive above 7. So maximum at q = 3, f(3) = 27 − 135 + 189 = 81; minimum at q = 7, f(7) = 343 − 735 + 441 = 49. (b) f″(q) = 6q − 30 = 0 → q = 5; f″ < 0 below 5 (concave), f″ > 0 above (convex). Inflection at (5, 65): f(5) = 125 − 375 + 315 = 65. (c) Sketch: through the origin (the only zero, since q² − 15q + 63 has no real roots), up to the peak (3, 81), concave down to (5, 65) where it straightens, convex down to the trough (7, 49), then up without bound. The inflection sits between the two turning points, as it must.
R15. (a) 9,000(1 + 0.05 × 6) = 9,000 × 1.30 = **€11,700.00**. (b) 9,000 × 1.05⁶ = 9,000 × 1.340096 = **€12,060.86**. (c) 9,000 × (1 + 0.05/4)^{24} = 9,000 × 1.0125^{24} = 9,000 × 1.347351 = **€12,126.16**. Simple interest never pays interest on interest; annual compounding does once a year; quarterly does four times, so the interest starts earning sooner.
R16. (i) the first. EAR = (1 + 0.07/4)⁴ − 1 = 1.0175⁴ − 1 = **7.19%** > 7.10%. Compare on the effective rate, never on the nominal.
R17. (a) 30,000 / 1.06⁴ = 30,000 / 1.262477 = **€23,762.81**. (b) 4,000 × (1 − 1.06⁻⁵)/0.06 = 4,000 × 4.212364 = **€16,849.46**. (c) 4,000 / 0.06 = **€66,666.67**. The five-year annuity is a quarter of the perpetuity because the perpetuity is the limit n → ∞ of the annuity formula: the (1 + r)⁻ⁿ term goes to zero, and the payments after year 5, though each small, are infinitely many — discounting shrinks them, it does not delete them.

(c) At 14%: factors 0.877193, 0.769468, 0.674972, 0.592080 → PVs 131,578.95 + 138,504.16 + 134,994.30 + 71,049.63 = 476,127.04 → NPV = −23,872.96, reject. R19. (a) WACC = 0.5 × 11% + 0.5 × 5% × (1 − 0.30) = 5.5% + 1.75% = **7.25%**. (b) Interest paid to the bank is deducted before tax is computed, so every euro of interest saves 30 cents of tax: debt effectively costs 5% × 0.7 = 3.5%. Dividends to shareholders are paid out of after-tax profit, so there is no such saving on the equity side.
R20. (ii) B is cheaper. Monthly compounding charges interest on interest twelve times a year, so A’s effective rate exceeds its nominal rate while B’s equals it. What is good for the depositor is bad for the borrower.
R21. (ii) falls. PV = 1,000/(1 + r)^{10}: the denominator grows with r. At 5% the value is €613.91, at 8% it is €463.19. The €1,000 is unchanged; what it is worth today is not.
R22. (ii) halves. PV = C/r; doubling r halves the fraction exactly. (From 5% to 10%: €120,000 to €60,000.)
R23. (i) a maximum. A zero first derivative makes it stationary; a negative second derivative means the curve is concave there, so the stationary point is a peak. It would be an inflection only if f″ were zero and changed sign.





R12, R13, R14, R2, R5, R8 are the midterm: domain, sign, derivatives, the maximum proved with the second derivative, convexity, the sketch, and the sentence for the Board. R13 has the exact shape of the case with other numbers.
R6, R7, R9, R10, R11 are the five items of the final exam’s calculus question, in the form they take there. If you can do these five cold in twenty minutes, that question is yours.
R15–R23 are the financial-mathematics block of the resit (multiple choice with a one-line justification) and the NPV decision; R18 and R19 are the pair that session 5 builds the bond on.

The inflection sits between the two turning points, as it must.
R15. (a) 9,000(1 + 0.05 × 6) = 9,000 × 1.30 = **€11,700.00**. (b) 9,000 × 1.05⁶ = 9,000 × 1.340096 = **€12,060.86**. Simple interest never pays interest on interest; annual compounding does once a year; quarterly does four times, so the interest starts earning sooner.

title: Revision set — weeks 1 to 4
text:
R12, R13, R14, R2, R5, R8 are the midterm: domain, sign, derivatives, the maximum proved with the second derivative, convexity, the sketch, and the sentence for the Board. R13 has the exact shape of the case with other numbers.

title: Week 2 — Drills
text:
Exam format. Show all work. Core items are for everyone; stretch items for whoever finishes early. Solutions at the end, worked the way an examiner wants to see them.


D1 (core). For each function, state the domain as an interval and say what the restriction means for the firm. (a) f(q) = √(q − 20) — profit per bike above a minimum run. (b) g(q) = ln(q − 5) — a log revenue that only starts once five units are sold. (c) h(q) = 120 / (q − 40) — average fixed cost per bike above capacity 40.
D2 (core). Arno Bikes faces demand p(q) = 1600 − 4q. (a) Write revenue R(q) and simplify. (b) Write profit π(q) using C(q) = 60,000 + 400q. (c) Evaluate π(100) and π(200). Which quantity is better, and by how much?
D3 (stretch). A second firm has R(q) = 30 ln(q + 1) (€ thousand) and C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25. (a) State the domain of R for q ≥ 0. (b) Compute π(5) and π(10) to two decimals.
D3b (added 22 October — the first lines of the midterm study). A third firm: C(q) = 0.6q² + 4q + 15 and R(q) = 25 ln(0.5q + 1), both in € thousand. (a) For each function give the domain algebraically and economically, as intervals. (b) Find where each meets the y-axis and the x-axis. Name the y-intercept of C in business terms. (c) C is a parabola. Where is its vertex, and is it the firm’s minimum cost? Say why in one sentence.



D4 (core). Evaluate, showing the factoring step: (a) lim (q→10) (q² − 100)/(q − 10) (b) lim (q→3) (q² − 5q + 6)/(q − 3)
D5 (core — exam form). Evaluate the one-sided limit lim (q→1⁺) (q − 1)²/(q − q²). Hint: factor the denominator first. Note the sign of each factor as q approaches 1 from above.
D6 (core). Evaluate the limits at infinity and say what each means for the firm: (a) lim (q→∞) (1200q − 4q²)/(q² ) (b) lim (q→∞) (60,000 + 400q)/q — average cost per bike as the run gets long.
D7 (stretch). lim (q→−∞) (3q³ − 2q + 1)/(5q³ + q²).
D7b (added 22 October — slant asymptotes). For each function, compute m = lim (q→∞) f(q)/q and, where m is finite and not zero, b = lim (q→∞) (f(q) − mq). State whether there is a slant asymptote and write its equation. (a) C(q) = 0.6q² + 4q + 15 (b) R(q) = 25 ln(0.5q + 1) (c) AC(q) = C(q)/q (d) f(x) = (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x + 1)



D8 (core). Differentiate, term by term: (a) π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000 (b) C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25 (c) R(q) = 30 ln(q + 1) (d) f(q) = 5q³ − 2q² + 7q − 1
D8b (core — one inside another). Differentiate, naming the inside each time: (a) ln(q + 1) (b) ln(5q) (c) (3q − 4)⁵ (d) e^(0.08t) (e) 20 ln(2q + 7)
D9 (core — the point of the week). For π(q) = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000: (a) Compute π'(80) and say, in one sentence a manager would use, what it means. (b) Compute π'(200) and do the same. (c) Solve π'(q) = 0. Compare with the vertex you found in week 1.
D10 (stretch). Using the definition, f'(a) = lim (h→0) [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, show that the derivative of f(q) = 3q² at q = a is 6a.



D11 (core — exam form). Find f(q) given f'(q) = 6q² − 2q and f(1) = 4.
D12 (core). Find the total cost function given marginal cost MC(q) = 0.8q + 3 and fixed cost C(0) = 25.
D13 (core — exam form). Integrate term by term; split the fraction first where there is one. (a) ∫ (6q² − 4q + 1) dq (b) ∫ (3q³ + 4q² − 2)/q dq



Solutions

D1. (a) Need q − 20 ≥ 0 → [20, +∞). Below 20 bikes the formula has no meaning: the firm does not operate under a 20-bike run. (b) Need q − 5 > 0 (strict: ln 0 is undefined) → (5, +∞). Revenue only exists past the fifth unit. (c) Need q − 40 ≠ 0 → (−∞, 40) ∪ (40, +∞); for a quantity, [0, 40) ∪ (40, +∞). At exactly capacity the expression blows up — the model breaks there.
D2. (a) R(q) = (1600 − 4q)q = 1600q − 4q². (b) π(q) = 1600q − 4q² − 60,000 − 400q = −4q² + 1200q − 60,000. (c) π(100) = −40,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 = €20,000. π(200) = −160,000 + 240,000 − 60,000 = €20,000. Equal. Two different quantities, the same profit — the parabola is symmetric about q = 150. Say this out loud: “more” is not the question, “where on the hill” is.
D3. (a) q + 1 > 0 → q > −1, so for a quantity the whole of [0, +∞). (b) π(5) = 30 ln 6 − (0.4·25 + 15 + 25) = 53.75 − 50 = €3.75k. π(10) = 30 ln 11 − (40 + 30 + 25) = 71.94 − 95 = −€23.06k. The second firm is past its best scale at 10.
D3b. (a) C: algebraically (−∞, +∞), a polynomial is defined everywhere; economically [0, +∞), output cannot be negative. R: algebraically 0.5q + 1 > 0 → q > −2, so (−2, +∞); economically [0, +∞). (b) C(0) = 15: the y-intercept is (0, 15), the fixed cost, €15k paid at zero output. x-axis: 0.6q² + 4q + 15 = 0 has Δ = 16 − 36 = −20 < 0, so no real zero: cost is positive everywhere. R(0) = 25 ln 1 = 0: the curve passes through the origin. ln(0.5q + 1) = 0 → 0.5q + 1 = 1 → q = 0: the origin is the only zero. (c) Vertex at q = −b/(2a) = −4/1.2 = −10/3 ≈ −3.33, where C = 25/3 ≈ 8.33. It lies outside the economic domain, so it is not the firm’s minimum: on [0, +∞) cost only rises, and the smallest cost the firm can face is the fixed cost at q = 0.
D4. (a) (q² − 100)/(q − 10) = (q − 10)(q + 10)/(q − 10) = q + 10 → **20**. (b) (q² − 5q + 6)/(q − 3) = (q − 3)(q − 2)/(q − 3) = q − 2 → **1**.
D5. Factor: (q − 1)² / (q(1 − q)). Now 1 − q = −(q − 1), so the expression is (q − 1)² / (−q(q − 1)) = −(q − 1)/q. As q → 1⁺, (q − 1) → 0⁺ and q → 1, so the value → −0 = **0**. The exam wants the factoring and the sign discussion written out, not just the answer.
D6. (a) Divide numerator and denominator by q²: (1200/q − 4)/1 → **−4**. Far out, profit falls like −4q²: the quadratic term dominates and the firm is deep in loss. (b) (60,000 + 400q)/q = 60,000/q + 400 → **400**. Average cost per bike settles at the variable cost: fixed cost spreads to nothing. This is economies of scale in one line.
D7. Divide by q³: (3 − 2/q² + 1/q³)/(5 + 1/q) → **3/5**.
D7b. (a) C(q)/q = 0.6q + 4 + 15/q → +∞. m is infinite: no slant asymptote. (b) R(q)/q → 0 (a log grows more slowly than any line), so m = 0; but R(q) → +∞, so there is no horizontal asymptote either. None: revenue grows without bound, ever more slowly. (c) AC(q) = 0.6q + 4 + 15/q. m = lim (0.6 + 4/q + 15/q²) = 0.6; b = lim (4 + 15/q) = 4. Slant asymptote y = 0.6q + 4: far out, the fixed cost shared per unit vanishes. (Also a vertical asymptote at q = 0, from the right: AC → +∞.) (d) m = lim (2x² + 3x − 1)/(x² + x) = 2. f(x) − 2x = (2x² + 3x − 1 − 2x² − 2x)/(x + 1) = (x − 1)/(x + 1) → 1. Slant asymptote y = 2x + 1, and a vertical one at x = −1.
D8. (a) π'(q) = −8q + 1200 (b) C'(q) = 0.8q + 3 (c) R'(q) = 30/(q + 1) (d) f'(q) = 15q² − 4q + 7
D8b. Outside first, inside untouched, then times the inside’s derivative. (a) inside q + 1, derivative 1 → 1/(q+1). The multiplication by 1 is why this one looks free. (b) inside 5q, derivative 5 → (1/5q)·5 = **1/q**. (Also visible from ln 5q = ln 5 + ln q, and ln 5 is a constant.) (c) outside (·)⁵, inside 3q − 4, derivative 3 → 5(3q−4)⁴·3 = **15(3q−4)⁴**. (d) inside 0.08t, derivative 0.08 → 0.08 e^(0.08t). (e) inside 2q + 7, derivative 2 → 20 · (1/(2q+7)) · 2 = **40/(2q+7)**.
D9. (a) π'(80) = −640 + 1200 = **+560**. At 80 bikes a month, one more bike adds about €560 to profit. Make more. (b) π'(200) = −1600 + 1200 = **−400**. At 200 bikes, one more bike costs about €400 of profit. Make fewer. (c) −8q + 1200 = 0 → q = 150, exactly the vertex −b/2a from week 1. The formula worked because the curve was a parabola; the derivative works whatever the curve.
D10. [3(a+h)² − 3a²]/h = [3a² + 6ah + 3h² − 3a²]/h = (6ah + 3h²)/h = 6a + 3h. As h → 0 this → 6a. Divide before letting h go: that is the whole trick.
D11. Antiderivative term by term: f(q) = 2q³ − q² + c. Then f(1) = 2 − 1 + c = 4 → c = 3, so f(q) = 2q³ − q² + 3. Never forget the constant: the initial condition is what pins it down, and the exam always gives you one.
D12. C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + c, and C(0) = c = 25, so C(q) = 0.4q² + 3q + 25. The constant of integration is the fixed cost. That is not a coincidence; it is the economics.
D13. (a) Power up and divide, term by term: 2q³ − 2q² + q + c. Check: differentiate and you get back 6q² − 4q + 1. (b) Divide each term by q first: 3q² + 4q − 2/q. Then integrate each piece: ∫ 3q² dq = q³, ∫ 4q dq = 2q², ∫ −2/q dq = −2 ln|q|, so q³ + 2q² − 2 ln|q| + c. The 1/q term is the only one the power rule cannot do (it would divide by zero): it is the log.
